How I saved $4,200 on 3 weeks in Portugal (without camping out) 
 This past January, I should have paid $6800 to go to Portugal. I ended up paying a total of $2,600. Here's how: 
 Flights: $1,850 savings 
 I had 68k Chase Sapphire Preferred points, plus a pile of United miles from business trips over 2 years. I checked mid Sept and they had a transfer bonus - 25% more points from Chase to United. Voila, my points became enough for a round trip saver flight from Newark to Lisbon. Ended up paying $121 in taxes/fees for a flight that was $982 in February (my dates) 
 I waited. I left Jan 9 and came back Jan 30. Europe flights in the Northeast tank after the holidays in mid winter. For June, it was over $1400 for the same itinerary. 
 Hotels/Apartments: $1,600 savings 
 3 weeks - 8 nights in Lisbon, 6 in Porto, 7 in Lagos (Algarve) No hotels - booked apartments on Booking.com in January, peak low season and hotel owners beg for any booking. $54 for my 1-bedroom in Alfama (Lisbon). If I booked for June, probably $150 for the same place. 
 Lagos, found guesthouse with an ocean view room for $47/night - breakfast included. Plus - booked via a credit card portal (booked thru Chase travel portal with Sapphire card, effectively got another 5% for points via this). 
 Everything else: $750+ savings 
 Museums - Lisbon card (€42 for 72 hours) got me into Jeronimos Monastery, Belem Tower, transit. ~€60 value. 
 Off season tours - did wine tour to Douro Valley from Porto. €55. Instead of €85 in summer. Also only 6 of us instead of a van full 
 Eating - no reservations at Taberna da Rua das Flores in Lisbon (Jan) - I walked in on a Tuesday. No tourist markups. Same dinner. 
 Trade offs (no BS) 
 It rained 4 days in Porto. Some beach restaurants closed in Lagos. Short days. Sunset around 5:30. Portugal in Jan was still 60 degrees in Lisbon in the afternoon most days. Pena Palace in Sintra, I had it to myself (almost) on a Wednesday morning. Summer it's a 2 hour line. 
 Total 
 Flights: $1,850 savings Hotels: $1,600 Tours/Attractions: $750 Total: $4,200. That's my next trip covered. Which I'm planning. Greece in November anyone?

How I Saved $4,200 on Three Weeks in Portugal (Without Sacrificing) 
 This past January I should have paid $6,800 for my Portugal trip. I ended up paying $2,600. Here's how: 
 FLIGHTS: Save $1,850 
 I'd accumulated 68,000 Chase Sapphire Preferred points and enough United miles from business travel over the last couple of years. In the middle of September, I discovered a 25% transfer bonus: Chase would give me 25% more points when transferring them to United. Suddenly I had enough points for a roundtrip saver award from Newark to Lisbon. I ponied up $121 in taxes and fees for a flight that would go for $982 in February—when I'd be there. 
 The trick was timing. I went January 9th - January 30th. After the holidays, mid-winter airfare to Europe from the northeast is cheap as hell. It was more than $1,400 in June for the same trip. 
 LODGING: Save $1,600 
 For the three weeks, I stayed eight nights in Lisbon, six in Porto, and seven in Lagos (in the Algarve). I didn't stay in hotels. Instead, in January (peak low season when property owners are desperate for business), I reserved apartments on Booking.com. $54 a night for a one-bedroom apartment in the Alfama neighborhood of Lisbon. If I'd done the same thing in June, I would have paid, what, $150? 
 In Lagos, I got a guesthouse with a room overlooking the ocean for $47 a night, including breakfast. The icing on the cake was that I used a credit card portal: by booking through the Chase travel portal with my Sapphire card, I basically got another 5% back in points. 
 THE REST: Save $750+ 
 MUSEUMS: I got the Lisbon Card (€42, 72 hours). I saw the Jerónimos Monastery. I saw the Belém Tower. And, hey, I could ride public transportation. I saved about €60. 
 OFF-SEASON TOURS: Porto to the Douro Valley for a wine tour. I paid €55 instead of €85 in the summer. And it was just six of us instead of a packed-out van. 
 FOOD: No, I didn't make reservations at Taberna da Rua das Flores in Lisbon in January. I just walked in on a Tuesday night. Same dinner. No inflated tourist prices. 
 HMM, THE NEGATIVE THINGS (BEING HONEST) 
 It rained for four days in Porto. There were a few beach restaurants closed in Lagos. Short days: sunset at 5:30pm. But you know what? It was 60°F in Lisbon most afternoons in January in Portugal. And I had nearly all of the Pena Palace in Sintra on a Wednesday morning to myself. That's a two-hour line in the summer. 
 TOTALS 
 FLIGHTS: $1,850 saved 
 LODGING: $1,600 
 TOURS/ATTRACTIONS: $750 
 TOTAL: $4,200. That's enough to go on my next trip. I'm already planning that. Greece in November. Anybody?

blog_personal_02_sonnet.text:
I think my garage will always smell like PB Blaster now.
I bought it August 2nd off a guy named Russ in Hillsboro. He had it under a tarp since 2011. 1978 Honda CB750K. 31400 miles. Matte finish due to dust. $1400 cash. Odometer cable is stuck, carbs rock solid due to varnish, and a family has been living in the airbox. It's the typical 10 year first owner situation. 
 First week was all about degreasing. I burned through 4 cans of Simple Green and a Saturday trying to remove 11 years of crud on the engine cases. So I can actually get an idea what I'm looking at. I'm pretty excited to find that the engine cases are in great condition. No cracks. No stripped threads. Just surface oxidation on the fins. 
 So 2nd week. Took out carb bank (4x Keihin CV carburetors) let them soak in Berryman's dip for 3 days. Rebuilt with CB750 Supply carb kit. $89 for all 4 sets of gaskets, o-rings, and float valves. It was the most awesome afternoon I've had working on this so far. Seeing the float bowls with a crust crack open again. 
 So far for money (I'm keeping track in a book on the workbench...)
 Bike - $1400
 Carb kit - $89
 Battery (YB9-B. The old one was a brick.) $34
 New fuel lines and inline fuel filter. $22
 Degreaser, brushes, gloves, shop rags. Around $60 I guess
 NGK plugs set of 4. $18
 Total as of tonight, September 20th is $1623. 
 Comp test was 145, 148, 142, 140psi on all 4. Which on a 48 year old air cooled engine made me feel like I hit the lottery. Haven't tried to start it yet. That's the goal for next weekend. Have fresh fuel in the tank. Get points gapped. My neighbor Dave has rebuilt 2 of these. He keeps saying don't rush the first kick... I'm rushing.

blog_personal_04_luna.text:
January 8, 2025. Age 51. I tie up my running shoes, ready to complete my first half marathon with a titanium knee.

In the past, this seemed laughable. I had my right knee replaced in March 2024 after years of arthritis made every step up stairs, on long walks, and even to step out of the car an awful experience. Rehab was brutal, but also humbling. Sacramento, CA-based physical therapist Elena Morales had me start walking around my neighborhood for 5 minutes at a time. Two miles at a time by June. On the stationary bike, with strength work, 3 times a week in September.

Still no running. Then I get a message from friend Marcus who tells me about the Davis Turkey Trot Half Marathon. November 27, 2025. "You don't have to run the whole way," he says. "You just need to train regularly."

So I start with a walk-jog schedule. Jog 1 minute. Walk 2 minutes. Do that for 20 minutes. My first run is a measly 1.4 miles. My knee swells up afterward. Ice it. Call Elena. Learn the hard lesson that improvement doesn't necessarily equal pushing through pain.

These days, I train 4x per week. Slow jogs 2x per week on Tuesday. Strength work on Thursday. Long, slower distance on Saturday. Stretch and recover on Sunday. Build the long distance each week (no more than half-a-mile increase each week). 3 miles in February. 6 miles in April. 9 miles along the American River Parkway last Saturday in 2:11.

No PRs here. Just want to finish the half marathon in Davis, before it's closed for the day, and ideally with a smile and the ability to still walk. I realize I won't be going at the pace I would have gone when I was 30. (Not because I ran when I was 30.) But each mile is a reminder that my body still has surprises in store.

Me. 51. With a titanium knee. And a very slow-cooked training regimen. Learn that sometimes starting over can be pretty amazing.

January 8, 2025. 51 years old. I tied my running shoes, eager to complete my first half marathon post knee replacement.

Crazy, right? Me a runner?  Not a year ago. In March 2024 I got my right knee replaced. For a long time arthritis had made climbing stairs and taking long walks and getting in and out of the car torturous.  As recovery stretched on, it was humbling. My PT (Elena Morales) had me start slow with five minute walks around my neighborhood in Sacramento, CA. In June I could walk two miles without stopping. September I began stationary biking and strength training three times a week. 

Run? Forget about it. Until my friend Marcus brought up the Davis Turkey Trot Half Marathon. He said it would take place on November 27, 2025. “You don’t have to run the whole way. Just have to stay consistent.”

 So I started with a walk/run combo. One minute jogging, two minutes walking for 20 minutes. First run was 1.4 miles. My knee was swollen. I iced it. Called Elena. And learned an important lesson: improvement doesn’t always mean pushing through pain. 

I now run four times a week. On Tuesdays I do low intensity walk runs. Thursdays are strength. On Saturdays I run longer but slower. Sunday’s I stretch and recover. I'm only increasing long runs by half mile per week. I ran three miles in February. In April I did six. Last Saturday I ran nine miles down the American River Parkway in two hours and eleven minutes. 

I’m not trying to set a record. I want to finish in Davis before the run ends. And hopefully with a smile on my face and the ability to walk afterwards. And of course I’ll run slower than I did in my 30’s (cause I didn’t run in my 30’s.) But every mile is like…I’m a wonder to my body! 

At 51, with a titanium knee and a lot of patience with my training, I’m discovering that sometimes starting over is a win.

blog_personal_06_glm.text:
Co-Parenting a Family with a 6-Hour Time Difference: Navigating School Events in Berlin and Toronto

When Marcus started his job teaching at Humboldt University in September 2023, we knew our co-parenting journey was about to become a lot more challenging. He moved to Berlin. I remained in Toronto with our two children, Elena (11) and Theo (8). Six hours. That doesn't seem like much of a time difference. Until you're trying to coordinate a parent-teacher night.

Here's what we've learned after 18 months of this.

Our shared calendar is our lifeline. All of it goes in the one Google Calendar. School stuff. Swimming lessons at Wallace Emerson Community Centre. Theo's Wednesday speech therapy (4pm Toronto time). If it's not on the calendar, it didn't happen. Marcus checks it with his morning coffee at 7am in Berlin (1am for me) so he sees anything I've got going on in the evening before I even wake up.

We take turns with events. Marcus can't physically be in the gym at Earl Grey Public School, but he can still participate in parent-teacher interviews by video. Often that's at 8 or 9pm his time. Elena's teachers have been great at booking her in earlier. For the stuff we really need to be there for (the winter concert, picking up March break), he flies over. He's been back four times now, staying in a rental close to us on Dovercourt Road.

Tuesdays and Fridays are "Berlin dinner" for the kids. (2:30pm his time, so he's having lunch when they're having dinner.) They talk about their week. Marcus has Theo show him his LEGO creations on camera. Elena mostly just rolls her eyes, but never misses it. We're very protective of this time. No playdates scheduled during it.

It's been tough sometimes. When Theo was sick with the flu last February and I was up all night, Marcus felt powerless 6,600km away. We've learned there are ways he can still help. He can manage all the online things (ordering school supplies, booking appointments for Theo's therapy, looking into March break camps) from abroad. It's help. It's still help.

The kids have this weird math skill now with time zones. Theo can calculate the time in Berlin from Toronto in his head faster than I can. There are times when it's daylight savings different times (Europe switches two weeks earlier than North America in the spring) and it's a fortnight of five hours and everyone's confused.

We didn't expect our co-parenting set-up to look like this when we broke up in 2021. But when Elena was talking to her school counsellor recently, she said she had "a dad in two countries." She sounded so impressed. Like it was his superpower. I'll take that.

Do the same stuff: shared calendar, blocked times for calls, divide up the invisible work by continent. It's not ideal. But it's ours.

LONG DISTANCE CO-PARENTING (Navigating school from Berlin and Toronto)

In September 2023, Marcus got a new job teaching at Humboldt University. This meant co-parenting was about to become a headache. Marcus would be in Berlin. I would be in Toronto with Elena (11) and Theo (8). Six time zones? No problem! At least not when it comes to parent-teacher night.

So here’s what we’ve learned in 18 months of this.

CALENDAR KINGDOM

We’re in a single Google Calendar together. Everything from school activities to Wallace Emerson Community Centre swim time to Theo’s speech therapy every Wednesday at 4 pm Toronto. (No calendar entry = it didn’t happen.) Marcus reviews calendar with morning coffee at 7 am Berlin time (1 am here). So he catches what I’m doing the night before before I even wake up.

WHICH PARENT FOR WHICH EVENT

Marcus can’t exactly sit in the gym at Earl Grey Public School, but he video calls in for parent-teacher (generally 8-9 pm Berlin time). Teachers for Elena have been pretty accommodating with early appointments. When we really do need someone there (winter concert, March Break pickup) Marcus flies in. He’s been there four times (stays in a rental place near us on Dovercourt Rd).

BERLIN DINNERS (Tues/Fri)

That’s 2:30 pm for Marcus. So he has lunch when they have dinner. They chat about their week. (Theo’s favourite is to show off LEGO creations on camera. Elena eye-rolls a lot but never skips.) We are very protective of this time. (No playdates during dinner.)

TOUGH TIMES

Marcus felt helpless 6,600 km away when Theo got the flu last February and I was up all night. We’ve learned he can still be helpful. He does all the online stuff (buy school supplies, schedule Theo therapy, search for March Break camps) from there. Practical help is helpful.

MATH NERDS

The kids are weirdly good at the Berlin-Toronto time difference. (Theo is quicker at converting Toronto to Berlin than I am.) Daylight savings (Europe has this two weeks before North America in spring) means there’s a fortnight of 5-hour difference. Confusion reigns!

It’s not the co-parenting scenario we planned in 2021 when we broke up. But Elena recently told the school counsellor that she has “a dad in two countries.” And she made it sound cool. I’ll take it.

If you’re in this kind of situation: Use the same calendar. Set aside time for calls. Divide invisible labour across hemispheres. It’s not perfect but it’s our own.

Punch out of my last St. Luke's Medical Center shift (Tuesday in July of 2024), start UX bootcamp the following Monday. 
 14 months later, 3 weeks into a product design job at a healthtech startup in providence. I wanna write this shit down because the arc I thought it would follow initially didn't resemble the arc I followed at all. 
  Months 1-3, GA part time UX/UI course, in addition to working 3 12 hour night shifts at the hospital per week. So clock out at 7am, sleep till 1pm, join the 3pm gang call for the cohort. Finished two projects during this time period. 
Redesigning my hospital's patient discharge instructions (apparently horrible. 
Wow. 
When you look at it as a designer instead of just as a nurse handing the shit out). 
 Also did a medication reminder app called Dosewise. 
  Months 4-7, rough times. 
 November of 2024 I said fuck it I'm out of nursing. (we'd saved money for 8 months of expenses for this exact purpose). 
Just informational interviews the whole time. 
34 of them. 
Spreadsheet them. 
Usually via the providence ux meetup I found called ocean state ux that happens the second thurs of every month at a coworking place on westminster st. 
 Got portfolio feedback sessions with 11 people from those calls. 
  Months 8-10, finished up another (unsolicited) case study. 
Redesigning the nurse handoff for my old hospital, interviewed 6 of my old coworkers to learn where things fall through the cracks during shift changes. 
This one got way more callback interviews than the other 2 cause this is the one where my nursing knowledge is the thing I'm using, not the thing I have to negate. 
  Months 11-14 
61 applications, 9 1st interviews, 3 final interviews, 1 offer. 
Offer came from a 40 person company making software for home health aids called Verve health. 
 Sept 2, 2025. 
$89k starting salary. 
This is like $6k less than my last year of nursing with all the differentials but no more nights. 
  For anybody beginning: prepare for month 5-7 to be like "what the hell man is this shit ever gonna happen" 
It's not nothing, it's just snowball of interviews.

blog_personal_10_luna.text:
Eli was 8 when we started homeschooling him in September of 2022. Reading at about a 1st grade level, with dyslexia, every worksheet was a test that he had already failed. He could draw a picture that told the whole story about the water cycle. He would get stressed and embarrassed after struggling to read a short paragraph on the topic. 
 We used three of the 'popular' language arts products that first year. One heavy on independent reading. One that went too quickly through spelling words. Each lasted only about six weeks. All About Reading Level 2 and All About Spelling was the program we needed. The 20 minute sessions were explicit when it came to phonograms, syllables, and blending. He was using letter tiles and saying them on the table. He was reading the books that could be decoded rather than guessing by the pictures. Eli was reading aloud simple chapter books by February 2023 without falling apart. 
 We used Institute for Excellence in Writing Primary Arts of Language for writing. I liked the separation of the physical act of writing from coming up with ideas. Initially, he would dictate to me as I typed the answers. Then he would copy one sentence. Then two sentences. And before long he was writing short paragraphs. His favorite was writing about the three little pigs from the wolf's perspective. 
 Math wasn't quite as much of a challenge. Word problems were an issue as the reading was a barrier to demonstrating understanding. We used Math-U-See as it was very hands on and concrete. We worked multiplication with colorful blocks for almost two months before writing the equations. I would read each word problem to him. He could draw it, or verbalize the thought process. 
 It's mainly about the pace. We are school for about three hours a day (focused) in the morning. Taking breaks every 25 minutes to get moving. We also stopped trying to align ourselves with the local school district's school year. Eli read a 120 page book on his own (adventure book) by May 2024. Yes, it took almost three weeks. But he read the book and then immediately wanted the next one! 
 We haven't cured his dyslexia, and it's not easy to homeschool. But the curricula we selected gave Eli the tools. More importantly, they let him know he could do it.

We homeschooled Eli starting at the age of 8 (Sept 2022) when he was reading at a 1st grade level. Dyslexia meant worksheets were like a test he had already failed. He could draw a picture to explain the water cycle in great detail, but when he'd read a short paragraph on the subject he was frustrated and ashamed. 
 We'd tried 3 different popular language art programs in our first year. One had an emphasis on independent reading. Another skipped spelling lists. We tried each one for 6 weeks or less. What we ended up sticking to was All About Reading Level 2. We paired it with All About Spelling. It was short (maybe 20 min) and very clear on phonograms and syllables and blending. There were letter tiles. There was tapping on the table. There was reading decodable books instead of visual guessing. By February 2023 we could listen to him read simple chapter books out loud without him shutting down. 
 For writing we did Institute for Excellence in Writing's Primary Arts of Language. I loved that this helped separate the physical process of writing from coming up with content. Eli would dictate to me for a while while I wrote out the answers. He slowly worked up to copying one sentence at a time. Then 2. Then writing a few paragraphs. His favorite thing to write about was retelling "The Three Little Pigs" from the point of view of the wolf. 
 Math wasn't as painful, but word problems were hard because the reading got in the way of demonstrating knowledge. We did Math-U-See, which we liked because of hands on and predictability. We worked on multiplication for almost 2 months with pretty colored blocks. Then we wrote out equations. I read every word problem to him. He could draw the problem or just tell me. 
 What helped us most was slowing down. We school for 3 focused hours in the morning (we take movement breaks every 25 min). We also stopped comparing to the school here. In May 2024 Eli read an entire 120 page adventure book independently. It took him almost 3 weeks, but he did it. Then he asked for the next one. 
 Dyslexia is still a thing and homeschooling is still hard work. But the right curriculum gave Eli tools without feeling like a burden. Better yet, they helped him recognize his own abilities.

blog_personal_12_glm.text:
Mom is 65 and asked for an upgrade to her bday party last June: 11 days of Tour du Mont Blanc hiking with her favorite son. Not the full 170km, she was quick to point out from the beginning. We'd do the standard French and Italian treks, skip a couple stretches with shuttle buses and knock down the daily hike distance from the typical 20+ to around 12 km/day. Best. Decision. Ever. 
 If you're venturing into the TMB world, be wary of those ultra-light freaks and 5am hikers on the forums. 
 Take some of the following to heart: 
 - PACKING. Mom went with 7 kg, I added 10 (we shared some first aid and of course, the (running) constant wine supply in Courmayeur). Her loadout: 1 40L pack, 2 merino hiking shirts, 1 convertible pants, rain jacket, down jacket and, most importantly, her own trekking poles. Got a knee replacement in 2021. Didn't leave without those poles. Mom said they restored 5 years to her legs. I went a bit overboard on shirts and ended up sending half of them back from Chamonix. 
 - PACE. Our Pact: only one big climb a day and that's it. On day 3, we almost died climbing from Les Contamines to Col du Bonhomme (2,329m). We took our lesson and revamped everything from there. Aim for 8:30 start time, plan to eat lunch at a refuge around noon. (Have the fucking tartiflette. Trust me.) Stop hiking around 3:30, so that Mom has a full hour of stretching and shower time before we begin the aperitif ritual. For refuge stays (e.g. Refuge Nant Borrant or Rifugio Bonatti), you'll need to reserve for July months in advance. Plan on March reservations. 
 - THE TRUTHS. Mom teared up at the viewpoint of Fenêtre d'Arpette. I did too. She took a couple days to ride the bus while I did the hiking (Chapieux to Courmayeur - no regrets. She was sipping esprsso in the village while I was trudging up Col de la Seigne in the rain.) Pace yourself. It's not failure. It is the key to the whole damn thing. 
 So if you're going to do this with an old parent, get the flexible plans for everything. And get a deck of cards. You'll be sitting around refuges for a while. Mom wrecked me at gin rummy every night. 
 Do it again? We've already circled the Walker's Haute Route for her 70th. She claims she's going to train for it. She will not. It will be ok.

Last June my mom turned 65 and instead of a party, she requested the best possible gift: 11 days hiking the Tour du Mont Blanc with me. Not the full 170km! She made that very clear from the beginning. We'd do the classic French and Italian parts, skip a few stages with buses, and average just 12km/day instead of 20+. And man, was that a smart choice. 
 
 On the TMB forums you will find ultralight and 5am warriors. They're not wrong. But what worked for us... 
 
 Packing. Mom's pack weight was 7kg and mine 10kg (that includes the combined first aid kit and our ever-increasing wine purchases in Courmayeur). Mom's gear: one 40L pack, 2x Merino hiking shirts, 1x Convertible pants, rain jacket, down jacket, and most importantly - her own trekking poles! (had a knee op in 2021 and said they gave her 5 more years in the legs.) I packed way too many shirts and sent half home from Chamonix. 
 
 Pace. One big climb a day. And that's it. Our almost-impossible climb out of Les Contamines to Col du Bonhomme (2,329m) on day 3 had us redesigning the whole thing. Get going by 8:30am. Stop at a refuge for lunch around noon. (Order the tartiflette, always) And get done walking by 3:30pm so Mom has a full hour to stretch and shower pre-aperitif. (e.g. Book months in advance for July at places like Refuge Nant Borrant and Rifugio Bonatti. Reserve by March.) 
 
 Real talk. She shed a few tears at the viewpoint of the Fenêtre d'Arpette and I did too, yeah. Also, 2 days she caught the bus while I hiked. (Les Chapieux to Courmayeur, whoops! She was drinking espressos in town while I was hacking up the Col de la Seigne in the rain.) And pace is not failure. In fact, pace is what made the whole thing even possible! 
 
 If you want to do this with an old parent, book the flexible version of everything. And bring a pack of cards. Cause it gets long in the refuges and she owned me every night at gin rummy. 
 
 Would I do it again? Well, we've already marked the Walker's Haute Route on her 70th calendar. She'll "train" this time... she won't. It'll be fine!

Two days after my 38th birthday, I impulsively enrolled in Clayworks on Fulton Street for the 6-week beginner wheel throwing class on a whim. My husband got it for me, as a joke, for my birthday. I never imagined I'd be doing this 14 months later.

My first bowl took 40 minutes to center. It looked like a beret. My teacher, a quiet guy named Marcus, 20-year wheel thrower said, 'The centering is 90% the battle. You don't get that week 1.' Well he was nice. I didn't get it until week 9.

I made sloped stuff for 4 months. I have an October mug that leans so far, you'd think it's pouring at rest. I kept it on my desk as a reminder. I didn't toss it. My wife dubbed my early works 'the Leaning Tower of Ceramics.'

In February, after a Tuesday night class. I made 4 matching cereal bowls. Same height. Same wall thickness. Thin enough to let light through the greenware. They actually matched. Marcus picked one up and said, 'Now you're not battling the clay anymore.' So I went home and kind of cried a little, like, over a bowl. Wow.

In June, I had a glaze I liked: A break-y white, iron speckled Shino glaze (breaks and does different things in every firing, depending on where it's placed in the kiln), and 40 things on a shelf, with no place to go. My 10-year old daughter suggested I sell at the farmers market on Saturdays in Wallingford. The one near our house. So I paid $35 for a 1/2 table for a morning in August.

I sold 11 pieces. 3 mugs. 4 small bowls. Butter dish. And 3 of the cereal speckled bowls I was most proud of. All to a lady replacing her entire set. $187. I've spent maybe 4x that on class costs this year. So, it's not a business. But I drove home and had an empty box in my trunk instead of a full one. That felt good.

I'm taking an intermediate class that starts in October. Marcus says it's time I learn to trim properly. I still have that beret bowl. I'm storing my keys in it.

I started taking the 6 week beginner wheel class at Clayworks on Fulton Street on a whim, 2 days after my 38th birthday. It was my husband's hilarious birthday gift. I never thought I'd still be there fourteen months later.

My first bowl that I got centered took 40 minutes and looked like a beret. My instructor (a quiet guy named Marcus who'd been throwing for 20 years) said "Remember, centering is 90% of the battle. You won't get it in week 1." He was just trying to cheer me up. I still didn't get it in week 9.

All my work in the first 4 months was crooked. I have a mug from October that's so crooked it looks like it's in the middle of pouring. I left it on my desk as a reminder instead of throwing it away. My wife started referring to my early works as "the Leaning Tower of Ceramics".

Then in February in a Tuesday night class I was able to throw a set of 4 matching cereal bowls. Same height. Same thickness of wall. Walls so thin you can see light through greenware. Marcus picked one up and said "Ok. You're not fighting the clay anymore." So I went home and cried a bit. That's weird about a bowl.

June comes and I've got a glaze that I like (a break-y, iron speckled white called Shino that does different things depending on where it is in the kiln in each firing) and 40 things sitting on a shelf with nowhere to go. My daughter (10) says maybe I should try the Farmers market on Saturdays in Wallingford. (There's one near our house.) So I pay $35 to have half a table for one morning in August.

I sell 11 things. Three mugs. Four little bowls. A butter dish. And three of those speckled cereal bowls I was so proud of. All to the same woman. She's replacing her whole set. I make $187. That's about 4x what I spent on classes this year. So it's not a business. But I came home with an empty box in the trunk instead of a full one. Feels like something.

I'm starting an intermediate class in October. Marcus says it's time I learned to trim right. I still have the beret bowl. Now I keep my keys in it.

Dear Professor Martinez,

I wanted to seek your guidance on how to properly understand the results of the Q3 regression in my economics term paper on "Changes in the Minimum Wage and Part-Time Employment in California from 2012 to 2023".

In my model, I find that a 10% rise in the real minimum wage is associated with an 0.8% fall in part-time employment (coefficient -0.080, p=0.03), accounting for county and year fixed effects, unemployment, and industry composition. However, in citing Freakley (2021), they found no significant drop in employment following changes in the minimum wage. At the moment, I claim in the paper that this is "consistent with a slight negative employment effect," but I'm afraid that this may clash with what the study that I cite found.

Is it better to present this as a clash, or as something explainable due to data/methodological differences? (Freakley is based on national quarterly data from 1990-2018. I'm looking at annual county-level California data from 2012-2023, with a specific focus on part-time employees. Without 2020-2021 in the data, the coefficient becomes insignificant. Perhaps this is due to labor market shocks from the pandemic?)

Do you think I should adjust the discussion to highlight these points and not necessarily claim a contradiction with Freakley?

Best, 
Jordan Lee

essay_opinion_01_luna.text:
Times Square should be car-free by 2030. And we should do it without spectacle—it's the logical evolution of New York City's bold and ongoing experiment with public space.

This isn't a new idea. In 2009, Mayor Michael Bloomberg closed Broadway to traffic through Times Square and started adding temporary pedestrian plazas from 42nd Street to 47th Street. Suddenly something new and exciting seemed routine. Pedestrian plazas minimized car-pedestrian conflicts. They gave pedestrians more space. They allowed more tables, performances, and simply standing still in the world's busiest neighborhood.

But Times Square is still a paradox. A place built to overload your senses. A place where millions of people gather every year. Where cars and trucks still cut through the crowds. Over 300,000 people cross through Times Square each day. Walking between barricades, truck drop-offs, cabs, buses, and turning vehicles. Meanwhile, advertising billboards promise New York as a place of endless possibilities.

When we finally make Times Square car-free, the goal should not be to remove all cars. We'll make exceptions for emergency services, utility vehicles, accessible transport, and planned deliveries. But we'll probably rule out private vehicles and most traffic cutting through the square. Other avenues like 7th Ave, 6th Ave, and 8th Ave will handle movement where it's needed. We'll be creating a public square that's not an island surrounded by cars and trucks. It'll be a public space for people.

This isn't just about what looks nice. A cleaner air. Fewer collisions. Less noise. Safer crosswalks. In a city where children and the elderly, workers and visitors share public space, that matters. And few places on this planet carry the right kind of symbolism for New York to make a point. Like New York values people over the ease of cutting through Midtown by car.

By 2030, we should build on the momentum we created in 2009. Make Times Square for the people who walk and work and perform and make it vibrant. Cars have enough roads. Let's give one square room to breathe.

We need to go car-free in Times Square by 2030, not as a gimmick, but as the logical extension of New York's longstanding effort to gain public space.

In 2009 under Mayor Michael Bloomberg, Broadway was made car-free through Times Square, and impromptu pedestrian plazas were added between 42nd and 47th streets. At first it seemed daring, then it became normal. The pedestrian plazas made it safer and more convenient for people to move around, without all the car-related congestion. They provided more space for pedestrians, and offered tables, performances, and the opportunity to simply stand still in one of the world's most densely populated areas.

But Times Square is a paradox. It's a place that's supposed to assault your senses— where millions of people visit every year. Yet cars and trucks can still zoom through. Thousands of people walk through Times Square every day—300,000 of them. They try to weave through barricades and trucks and cabs and buses and left-turning cars, while glancing at ads telling them what it means to live in New York, the city of possibilities.

A permanent, car-free Times Square doesn't mean we ban all cars, of course. We can still allow vehicles for emergency services, maintenance, accessible access, and thoughtfully time-scheduled deliveries. But private cars and through-traffic should be forbidden. We can continue to move on side avenues like Seventh and Sixth and Eighth Avenues. Times Square can become a plaza space that's truly civic, not just a pedestrian oasis amid all the machines.

This isn't just an issue of form. The reduction of pollutants, fewer accidents, less noise, and better crossings are all important in a city where we're all supposed to share space together, whether we're children, the elderly, workers, or visitors. Times Square is one of the few spots on the planet with enough symbolism to make a statement: New York values people over convenience and the ability to drive through Midtown.

By 2030, let's see through the changes that began in 2009. Times Square should primarily be a space for the people who walk through, work in, perform in, and breathe life into it. We have enough roads for cars. Let us let one breathe a little.

essay_opinion_03_glm.text:
I stumbled across a letter last march, tucked in a copy of Joan Didion’s *The White Album* that my mother sent me in 2019. The letter was 3 pages, handwritten, Oct 14th, 2019. Her minuscule, ever-so-slightly leaning-forward cursive: the dog of the neighbor, the cost of tomatoes at the saturday market in Davis California, her concerns that I wasn’t getting enough sleep in my Brooklyn apartment. I think i glanced at it and sent my mom a thumbs up. 
 A thumbs up that I can’t stop thinking about. 

I’m not some nostalgic old-timer. I love iMessage. Yesterday I sent 47 texts. Mostly jokes, mostly funny. I do not have a choice about the marvel that is the speed of digital communication. I would never give it up. But I’ve come to think the written letter is something we have quietly given up, but there is a place only a letter can go. 

When you write a letter it means something to the writer. The 3 pages my mom wrote her took maybe 40 minutes. Time is the only present you can’t trade-in or re-gift. When you write it by hand it’s clear you spent it. It’s there when your slightly squeezed lines come up to the edge. *I did it anyway*. With texts, it’s like, ‘I spent 4 seconds thinking about you.’ Sometimes that’s enough. Not always. 

Also: your letter is a thing. My mother’s letter traveled in an envelope, through the sorting system, across the country, and into a blue mailbox on 5th ave, and finally to my apartment. Her hand, literally, held the paper. I read it again when she passed away last June, and I could almost feel the force behind the pen. Try to find that emoji. 

So I started writing back before it was too late for her. I’ve been continuing to write. To my friend in Portland, Dana. To my old teacher in Chicago. One page a month. Max. That’s the point. It’s content-constrained. You can’t write a paragraph about the neighbor’s dog by hand and not say something. Because your wrist will say, 'enough.' Your heart, forced to work at the same tempo as the pen, says things that your thumb would never say. 

We’re not short of words. We’re short of slowness. A letter is just slow you can hold.

Her tiny sloping handwriting. The dog next door. Tomato prices on Saturday in Davis, CA. My sleep habits in my Brooklyn apartment, making her worried. I think I'd opened it and read it at some point. Thumbs-upped it to her via text.

I've been haunted by that thumbs-up ever since.

I'm no nostalgic. I love iMessage. I sent 47 texts yesterday. Mostly jokes. Mostly good ones. I love the instantaneous nature of digital communications. I wouldn't give it up. But I've realized that the handwritten letter is in a zone we can't enter otherwise. We've quietly conceded without realizing it.

The thing with a letter is it costs the writer. It took my mom about 40 minutes to write those three pages. Time is a gift we can't return. Or re-gift. Handwriting exposes the cost. The little squishy letters at the sides of the page say I kept going. A text says "I thought of you for four seconds." Sometimes that's enough. Not always.

But there's the physicality of it. That letter rode through envelopes. Through sorting centers. Across the country. Into the blue mail box on 5th Ave. To my apartment. My mom's hand held that paper. When she died in June last year I re-read it and could almost feel the pressure of her pen. What emoji is that?

Your heart, because it has to slow for the pen, will say things you can never say with the thumb.

We don't need words. We need slowness. A letter is just slow to hold.

My dad bought a Corolla in June of 1998 (4 months before I was born). It’s still running strong with 214,000 miles. It was from a Toyota dealer in Fresno that no longer exists. It still plays tapes. There’s a JCPenney receipt from 2003 stuck in the map pocket no one has ever dared take out. For reasons that could only be described as superstitious.

I spend $94.97 / month on stuff that doesn’t exist. Spotify. iCloud. ChatGPT Plus. A meditation app I opened 4 times. A New York Times subscription just for crosswords. Adobe. VPN. Amazon Prime (what the fuck is this anymore? It’s a tax, really). None of that stuff is like a car in that it depreciates. None of that stuff is going to exist in 2054 in any recognizable form. When the Corolla is old enough to pay for its own subscriptions.

You take care of a Corolla in a particular way. My dad changes the oil (himself, every 5000 miles) in the driveway, from a bucket that’s older than me. If it breaks he knows what broke. A timing belt. A knock sensor. He has opinions on NGK vs. Denso spark plugs. It’s an all-in relationship, but also, and critically, done. The moment he gave me the keys it was done. He has a thing he owns that doesn’t owe him shit.

The thing I own owes me the endless chore of maintenance, but in a different currency. Terms change. Prices gradually inch up from $9.99 to $12.99 with an email I don’t open. A feature I liked gets deprecated in exchange for something that costs more and is in a higher tier. It’s not me maintaining anything. I’m being maintained, in a way, by 14 different companies each of whom think they’ve got first dibs on my eyeballs and my card. A Corolla needs oil every few thousand miles. My subscriptions need something less, more often. They need a glance. A login. A renewal I don’t realize is coming up until my bank account catches me.

I thought it was the difference between owning and accessing. I think it’s more like: my dad’s car gets worse in ways he can anticipate and repair. My software gets “better” in ways I never wanted and can’t escape. He’s driving the same thing he was in 2004. I’m not using the same Spotify I was in 2019. The UI’s different. The algorithm’s different. The cost is different. All swapped out quietly under the same 4-letter name.

He’ll drive this thing until it dies. I can’t imagine ever being able to say that about anything I subscribe to on a monthly basis.

There’s a reason every city should do Bogotá’s Ciclovía Sundays. Not as an afterthought, but as a weekly exercise in public imagination.

Every Sunday and holiday, Bogotá blocks off about 140 kilometers of streets from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Cyclists, joggers, rollerbladers, stroller-pushing families, and elderly walkers flood through the roads normally dominated by cars. The custom started December 15, 1974, when a handful of citizen protesters blocked off some key streets. Today, up to a million may ride the routes in any given week. 50 years later.

The brilliance of Ciclovía is its simplicity. You don’t need a new subway line. Or a new sports arena. Or an electric bus fleet that looks like something from a sci-fi movie. All you need are barricades. And traffic cops. And public bathrooms. And first aid tents. And the political fortitude to declare, at least for 7 hours, that mobility and joy are more important than parking spaces.

I remember when I first watched video of what Bogotá’s Carrera Séptima turns into on Sundays. It wasn’t just a street for commuting. It felt more like a living room. You saw kids learning to balance on bikes. Young people trying out stunts. Grandparents holding hands. Juice and arepa vendors. The city hadn’t added any new parks. They just gave the one they had—the street—back to the people.

It’s an important point. So many urban initiatives are focused on transportation. How fast people can get downtown. How many cars can pass through a junction. How efficiently goods can circulate. Ciclovía is also about the function of being in a city without having to consume anything or go anywhere.

Someone will say the roads can’t be blocked off. It’s too disruptive. Yes, it is. Cities should balance competing interests. Not act like cars are the only legitimate residents of the streets. But what happens on Sundays is a low-cost test. A way to give people a glimpse of what it would feel like to have a less noisy, less dangerous street before debating any kind of redesign.

You can start with something simple. Just one avenue. For four hours. Once a month on a Sunday. And see what happens. People will show up. Not because they’ve been told to go exercise. But because they’ve been asked to feel like they belong.

Every city should emulate Bogotá’s Ciclovía Sundays, not as a gimmick but as a weekly exercise in municipal fantasy.

Every Sunday and holiday, Bogotá shuts down about 140 kilometers of streets for seven hours, from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Bikers, joggers, skaters, parents pushing prams, and walkers with arthritic knees crowd over boulevards that are normally for cars. The program started on December 15, 1974, when a handful of citizens organized a protest and blocked off a few roads in the city center. Half a century later the system could serve more than a million people in a typical week.

The genius of Ciclovía is that it’s not a big ask. You don’t need to build a subway extension, a new sports arena, or a futuristic bus line of electric vehicles. All you need are barriers, cops, toilets, first-aid posts, and the guts to say that for seven hours it’s more important to move and to enjoy than to park.

When I first saw videos of Bogotá’s Carrera Séptima on a Sunday, I was amazed at how it wasn’t just a road but a living room. Kids teetering on two wheels. Teens practicing their moves. Grandparents holding hands. Juice and arepa vendors. The city hadn’t created a new park, it had just given back the one it had—the street.

And it’s an important distinction. Most of what we think about when it comes to cities is mobility. How fast can we get people downtown? How many cars can we get across this intersection? How quickly can we transport our stuff? With Ciclovía you’re adding a different function: being a city without having to spend or move.

People will complain that this is too disruptive if you shut down the streets. Sure it is. Cities are supposed to be about reconciling, not ignoring the fact that cars aren’t the only people who have a right to be in public space. And what’s the harm in trying it out on a Sunday? It’s a way to let people see what it would be like to have a calmer, safer street before you get into discussions about redesigning it.

Any city can begin by taking one street and closing it for four hours once a month, on a Sunday. And then see what happens. People will show up, not because you’ve told them they need to exercise but because you’ve asked them to participate.

I have been going to the Met since I was nine and my grandmother gave me a couple of dollars and we stayed in the Egyptian section of the museum for the entire afternoon. That's what the place was for. So that kids from Queens could come and stand before a Temple of Dendur and feel like all of history was theirs too.

That's becoming increasingly expensive. In August 2022 the Met increased mandatory fees from $25 to $30 for out of state visitors. Then in 2025 it increased them to $35, one of the highest admission fees of any museum in the country. Technically the price for New York residents can be whatever you want, but it's a policy obscured by a whole lot of fine print. The kiosks are now prominently displaying the regular price. You have to know about this possible option to take advantage of it. And you have to be comfortable telling someone to your face that you'd like to give them $1. If you're a family of four from the Bronx, that's not a special. It's a tryout.

The leadership of the Met claims to need this because of the increased costs in the post pandemic era. They need to insure things. They need climate control for 2 million items. It's true that they don't have as much in their endowment as they used to. But come on. When they say "We need more money." Who are they really thinking of? Not the members of the board who go to all the fancy dinners. Not the tourists who can afford to spend $600 a night for a hotel and to them $35 is basically nothing. It's the bus of Newark kids, it's the day off nanny, it's the art student who used to sketch on Tuesdays.

One of the ways to judge a city is by what is available to the least fortunate people who live there. Central park is free. The Staten Island ferry is free. The Met was going to be that kind of place. A public space on public property leased from the city. With some public financing. And that $35 admission fee is saying the opposite of that. "Culture is a product. You are a consumer."

There's a way to fix it. The British Museum and the Tate in London have managed to keep their prices free in periods much more economically turbulent than the current ones. They've decided that it's necessary. The Met could try to do that. They could raise money in the endowment. They could get the city on board. Instead of just quietly making their museum more and more unaffordable for the people who need the museum.

Otherwise there's going to be a time very soon that a 9 year old girl from Queens will come up to those steps on 5th Avenue and her grandmother will look at the price and say, "Oh well." The Met will be diminished by it. And so will the city.

My 9-year-old daughter Maya had a birthday in March. Rather than giving her a smartphone, I bought her a flip phone.

It's a purple Nokia, with a plastic case that's all scratched up, a little screen, a battery that never seems to die. She uses it to call me if her soccer practice gets out early (at Lincoln Elementary), to text her grandma in Sacramento, to let me know she's walking to the library the three blocks from our apartment on Saturdays. That's pretty much it.

This wasn't anti-technology. Technology is part of Maya's life. She's got a Chromebook at school, and she's watching science videos, and knows how to ask Alexa for the weather. The thing I wanted to put off is a certain kind of technology, the kind that comes with a smartphone: the constant flow of notifications, videos, games, ads, social comparisons, adult attention.

At age 9, Maya is still learning how to be bored. When she's riding the bus on her way to swimming lessons, she's staring out the window. She sees the mural on 14th Street, the guy selling oranges near the station, whether you can see the moon from between the buildings. Last week she was trying to figure out a card trick by herself for 20 minutes because she had nothing else to do. I don't want to pre-empt all those empty spaces before she has a chance to find out what could grow there.

And it feels so much more deliberate when someone has to communicate on a flip phone. If Maya calls me, she's got something to say. If I call her, she says "Hi, Dad," instead of looking down at the screen while playing some game. We have a family rule about phones being put in backpacks at mealtime, and her phone is usually off by 7:30 p.m. I don't have to moderate a group chat or watch a social media account or explain why someone's vacation video has 400 likes.

But the flip phone sucks, obviously. She can't easily send pictures, or look at maps, or use the messaging app her friends like. Sometimes she complains that she's the only 4th grader who doesn't have an iPhone. I tell her that "not yet" is a complete sentence.

One day she'll have a smartphone. But right now I want her first phone to be a phone that helps her be independent, not a device that puts all of the internet in your pocket.

I know exactly how much I paid for my first record: $14.99, Tower Records on Sunset Blvd, April 2003. Radiohead’s Hail to the Thief. I listened to it so many times that summer, I can still picture the seam between 2 + 2 = 5 and Sit Down. Stand Up. I can still hear how one song ended and the next one started.

What did we lose? Money. Well, it was $14.99 so… for a fourteen-year-old it was money. But we lost the seam. The transitions. The place where bands decided: here’s what comes next.

Streaming got us everything (100 million+ songs on Spotify in 2024). And in return it removed all meaning from sequencing. Infinite music meant infinite playlists. The playlist became the algorithmic slot machine. Every Monday, Spotify’s Discover Weekly puts 30 songs in your ears. Most people, studies say, skip after 5 to 30 seconds. We don’t “listen.” We “audition.” All the time. Always. Forever.

An album was an argument. Abbey Road leads to The End. OK Computer knows where to put Fitter Happier, right there as a dead-eyed breather between Karma Police and Electioneering. Even a mixtape (I made dozens in high school, painstaking with a Sony dual deck) was a statement of love. You were deciding what came next. What came first mattered. Your playlist was a map of your soul. People could see the space between a Radiohead song and the Björk song you placed after it.

Now the queue is randomized by default. Enhance adds songs that the computer thinks belong there. Skipped. Skipped. Skipped. The typical Spotify user keeps returning to the same forty-ish songs each week, even with infinite music. The more choices, the less diverse taste.

I don’t want to get sentimental. Streaming is a miracle in many ways. A kid in Fresno can listen to Fela Kuti and Fugazi in the same afternoon. For free. But there’s an invisible price we paid for the abundance. Music used to be a commitment. Now it’s a stream you pass through, like the weather. Songs used to be events. Now they’re ambient.

My little protest: Every Friday night, I listen to one whole album from start to finish. No phone. No skips. Last week it was Alvvays’s Blue Rev. Fifty-one minutes, and it was more “listening” than the last six months.

We lost the seams. But we stopped seeing them.

I visit the Enoch Pratt Free Library on Cathedral St. in Baltimore nearly every Tuesday, and I have never been asked to pay for something to be there.

I know that shouldn't feel weird. But if you sat in any public space in America for three hours (Starbucks, mall food court, hotel lobby), how long do you think it would take for someone to ask you what you were paying for? The library is one of the last rooms in America where there is no fee for admission, and where the terms of service are: just be a person. Enoch Pratt doesn't require your zip code. The 73 branches of the Los Angeles Public Library don't require your immigration status. And when there was a wave of book bans in 2022, the Brooklyn Public Library gave away 6,600 free digital library cards to teenagers across the country, so they could read books that had been removed from their local library in, say, Texas or Florida.

Where can you go now? Well, the park bench, maybe, until they add those armrests that prevent you from sleeping (over 500 documented instances of hostile architecture in major US cities since 2014). Or the church (if you go). Or the DMV, which is a public institution, but not one you really hang out in. Elsewhere has all been silently metered - the mall is now a place you're being monitored by security guards on the property owner's dime; the sidewalk cafe demands $7 for your espresso cover charge; even the internet - long the great equalizer - now works with data brokers who sell your library adjacent Google searches to the advertisers. Libraries, meanwhile, are guided by the Library Bill of Rights, first approved by the American Library Association in 1939, which still says things should not be prohibited based on the origin or views of those who help create them.

This isn't by accident. Between 1883 and 1929, Andrew Carnegie built 1,689 library buildings in the U.S., and required communities to commit public tax dollars to making these free for all time, because - perhaps more than any other robber baron - he knew democracies needed rooms where you didn't have to pay a fee to rent your own citizenship.

According to Pew's 2024 survey, 61% of Americans went to a library or library website in the last year. That's more than voted in the last midterms. And it's not nostalgia, it's the last remaining commons. We should take note before we don't have.

In William Shakespeare's Macbeth, Act 5, Scene 1 Lady Macbeth's guilt is displayed through her sleepwalking, constantly washing her hands, and her broken speech. At first Lady Macbeth seemed strong and cold-hearted in the play. She encouraged Macbeth to kill King Duncan at Inverness, after the feast, Act 1. But now in Act 5, her conscience has taken over. The Doctor and the Gentlewoman are watching Lady Macbeth walk in with a candle. Clearly Lady Macbeth fears the dark and her guilt from the deeds she has committed. In her sleep Lady Macbeth gives the impression that she is reliving the killings of Duncan, Banquo and Lady Macduff. When she says, 'Out, damned spot!' this shows that Lady Macbeth thinks there is blood on her hands. The 'spot' may not actually exist physically but psychologically Lady Macbeth feels that this spot is always on her hands (guilty of Duncan's death). Earlier in the play Lady Macbeth said that 'a little water clears us of this deed'. However, in Scene 1 it is clear that this is not the case, Lady Macbeth's guilt does not just wash away like blood from our hands.

Lady Macbeth mentions how she remembers what happened when she said this, 'Who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?' This is about Duncan whose murder she saw as a practical problem. She also cries, 'The Thane of Fife had a wife; where is she now?' When she speaks of Lady Macduff's death who was killed by Macbeth's orders. It is clear that Lady Macbeth's guilt is now not only of her own actions but also the bloodshed Macbeth has committed in his reign. When the Gentlewoman says that Lady Macbeth has been washing her hands for fifteen minutes this is to show just how much her guilt has affected her mentally and physically. Lady Macbeth, unlike Macbeth, who copes with fear by ordering more killings is destroyed by the outcome of their ambition. Lady Macbeth is cut out of the court and even her own husband Macbeth who is facing the oncoming English army (Malcolm) near Dunsinane Castle. So Shakespeare shows Lady Macbeth's guilt as inescapable moral fate. Though she felt she was above conscience, her encouraged bloodshed has had a permanent effect on her mind.

In Act 5, Scene 1 of William Shakespeare's 'Macbeth', Lady Macbeth shows signs of guilt by walking in her sleep, washing her hands over and over, and by speaking in a confused manner. Unlike the fearless and evil Lady Macbeth of earlier in the play who encourages Macbeth to kill King Duncan at Inverness after the feast in Act 1, Lady Macbeth has now been completely overtaken by her guilty conscience. The Doctor and the Gentlewoman see Lady Macbeth walk in with a candle and point out that Lady Macbeth is terrified of the dark and the crimes that she helped commit. Lady Macbeth talks and acts as if she is replaying the murders of Duncan, Banquo, and Lady Macduff in her sleep, though she is asleep. She exclaims, 'Out, damned spot!' and reveals that she is imagining blood on her hands. While the actual 'spot' on her hands is not there, her guilt for the murder of Duncan is permanent and, psychologically, is the imaginary 'spot' on her hands. Earlier, Lady Macbeth declared that 'a little water clears us of this deed', but in this scene (Scene 1) her actions display that guilt cannot be washed off quite as easily as blood.

Moreover, Lady Macbeth speaks about the events and details of the crimes committed. She exclaims, 'Who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?' and is speaking about Duncan - the murder she earlier saw as a logistical concern. She also says 'The Thane of Fife had a wife; where is she now?' and is reminded of Lady Macduff's murder at Macbeth's bidding. These details show that Lady Macbeth is no longer only guilty of her crimes, but also of the bloodshed committed by Macbeth during his rule. The Gentlewoman states that Lady Macbeth has been washing her hands for the past fifteen minutes, highlighting that guilt has torn her mind and body. In contrast to Macbeth, who attempts to solve his problems by committing further murders out of fear, Lady Macbeth is wrecked by the results of their ambition. The guilt she experiences shuns her from the court, and even Macbeth himself, who battles the oncoming English soldiers with Malcolm in command near Dunsinane Castle. In this way, Shakespeare shows that Lady Macbeth is suffering in a way that cannot be avoided (morally), and she, once thought to be greater than guilt, has been irreparably affected by the bloodshed she condoned, destroying her mind.

Though often underestimated, the introduction of the Ford Model A on December 1927 was a major factor in driving the growth of American suburbs during the late 1920s and 1930s. The production of the ageing Model T ended in May 1927 and Ford closed their factories for six months for a change-over. When the Model A was introduced on December 2, 1927, it provided Americans with a new car that was faster, safer and more comfortable than the Model T. Priced from $385 (Roadster) to $1400 or so (Town Car), the Model A was within the price range of the middle class, but with the elegance that made longer daily driving trips possible. By 1931 more than four million Model A's had been sold, and by 1930 America had more than 23 million automobiles registered for a total population of approximately 123 million people.

This new ability to travel was changing the American landscape. People no longer had to live within walking distance of the factory or the trolley. Now they could easily drive 10 or 15 miles. The Model A's 65 mph maximum speed (compared to the Model T's 40-45 mph) made it possible to really enjoy a suburban commute to cities like Detroit, Chicago and Los Angeles. Developers of real estate noticed. In Los Angeles they were expanding sprawling subdivisions along new arterial roads. Developers selling homes to automobile owners who would commute, in the future Levittown-style communities on Long Island and Westchester County New York. Billboards actually advertised houses "twenty minutes from downtown."

The Federal Aid Highway Act of 1921 established a network of paved primary roads, and the local authorities paved the suburban roads as well, often issuing municipal bonds with the assumption that we were heading into an automobile society. This translated into buying habits; roadside businesses, diners, early shopping centres like Kansas City's Country Club Plaza (opened 1923, and built out in the late 1920s) catered to people who would now arrive in automobiles, rather than on the trolley.

Although construction slowed after 1929 due to the Great Depression, the pattern for suburbanization had been set. No other car of the time was so important in the transition from the utilitarian Model T to the mass-automobility of the post-war period. Millions of ordinary people were now able to have reliable, comfortable cars. The American dream was shifting from the row house near the trolley to a detached home on a suburban lot, with a driveway in front.

The introduction of the Ford Model A in December 1927 was a large but underappreciated factor in the boom in US suburbanization in the late 1920s and 1930s. When the old Model T finally stopped being built in May 1927, Ford closed the production lines for six months to retool for the new model. And when the Ford Model A was first unveiled on December 2, 1927, it introduced to Americans a car which was quicker, safer, and more comfortable than the Model T had been. Priced between about $385 (for the Roadster) and about $1400 (for the Town Car), the Model A was still within the budget of middle class families, and sufficiently refined to make longer driving commutes possible. By 1931 Ford had sold over four million Model A's, and by 1930 there were more than 23 million automobiles registered in the US (out of a population of around 123 million).

All of these automobiles changed the urban landscape. Suddenly, workers who had had to be within walking distance of a factory or streetcar could easily commute ten or fifteen miles. The Model A could go up to about 65 mph (the Model T was only 40-45 mph), which meant that it was possible to actually have a convenient commute to the city (say, from a suburb of Detroit or Chicago or Los Angeles). Property developers responded: in LA, massive subdivisions spread outward along new arterial roads; while in the proto-Levittown developments of Long Island and Westchester County, NY, developers started selling houses to the automobile commuter specifically. Advertisements on billboards encouraged people to buy houses "a 20 minute drive from downtown."

The federal government supported this process: in addition to the paved primary road network established by the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1921, local governments paved their own suburban roads, often issuing municipal bonds (which relied on auto-driven growth). Even shopping habits were affected as roadside shops and diners and early shopping centers like Kansas City's Country Club Plaza (1923, expanded into the late 1920s) began to target customers coming by car instead of streetcars.

After 1929, the Great Depression put the brakes on development, but it was too late: suburbanization had been set in motion. More than any other particular car of the age, the Model A marked the transition from the Model T's utilitarianism to the age of mass automobility in the post-war years. In normalizing the experience of having an affordable, reliable, and comfortable car for millions of ordinary families, the Model A helped shift the American dream from being in a row house near the trolley, to having a detached house on a suburban lot with a driveway in front.

In October 1973, Arab countries in the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, in response to U.S. support of Israel during the Yom Kippur War, reduced oil supplies and placed an embargo on the United States, the Netherlands, and other countries. In a matter of months the price of a barrel of oil increased from around $3 to nearly $12 by early 1974. The crisis sharply illustrated the dependence of the Western economies on a resource they did not control.

While the United States was an important oil producer, U.S. oil production reached its high point in 1970 and by 1973 the United States imported one-third of its oil. Western European and Japanese countries were even more dependent, importing most of their petroleum from the Middle East and North Africa. The oil embargo was felt almost immediately. In the United States, gasoline rationing was implemented, odd-even license plate restrictions were introduced so cars could be filled only on alternate days, long lines at gas stations formed, and a nationwide 55-mile-per-hour speed limit was introduced in early 1974 to save fuel. In Britain, the oil crisis and a coal miners' strike led to the adoption of a three-day industrial workweek. In Japan, which was importing more than 75% of its energy, there was panic buying of consumer goods and inflation, known as the "toilet paper panic" in 1973.

The economic effects of the embargo were serious and long-lasting. By 1974, U.S. inflation rose to over 12%, stock markets tumbled, and the age of cheap energy supporting postwar economic growth ended. The new phenomenon of "stagflation" (stagnant economies with inflation—rare in the past) seemed to defy conventional economic measures.

However, the embargo was also a wake-up call. The West created the International Energy Agency in 1974 to manage emergency stockpiles and lessen dependence. France began a huge expansion of nuclear power. Japan led the way in energy efficiency, becoming a world leader in energy-efficient technologies. Denmark began its shift to wind power. The embargo, in other words, showed the West dependence and the possibility of adjustment.

The 1973 oil embargo is an enduring case study of economic interdependence. A cartel of oil-producing nations using the resource as a political weapon could upset the most powerful world economies almost instantaneously. It was a reminder that energy security is national security and it has implications for foreign policy from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to current discussions of renewable energy and supply chains. The long lines at the gas pumps in 1973 were not just an annoyance. They were a warning that the West has never quite been able to ignore.

The impact of this shock was a brutal awakening to the extent to which the West had become reliant on a resource it didn’t control.

Japan, which imported over 75% of its energy, saw panic purchasing of consumer goods and inflation, later dubbed the “toilet paper panic” of 1973.

Economically, the effects were profound and long-lasting: in the US, inflation rose to over 12% by 1974; stock markets collapsed; and the age of cheap energy that powered postwar prosperity was over. Policymakers talked of “stagflation”—a hitherto rare blend of stagnant growth and inflation—that seemed impossible to treat with existing tools.

The embargo also brought awareness. The West set up the International Energy Agency in 1974 to coordinate emergency reserves and diminish vulnerability. France started a large nuclear power project. Japan focused on energy efficiency, and became a global leader in fuel-saving technology. Denmark started its journey towards wind power. This was the month that the Bureau of Labor Statistics finally validated our family's suspicions that began weeks prior - inflation had indeed increased by about 9.1% over the previous year, the highest level seen in forty years. For a family of five living in a medium-sized suburb in Ohio, this statistic was no longer a looming, abstract concept mentioned on our nightly news broadcasts. Instead, it became an itemized breakdown of what could and couldn't be purchased for our weekly sustenance.

Up until 2022, my mom's regular weekly shopping trip would run us about $180 for two carts worth of groceries. Come October, she was spending nearly $240 while cutting back to one cart. Egg prices, formerly $1.50 per dozen, rose well over $3.50 following an avian flu outbreak, only adding to the swelling inflation. The price of a gallon of milk rose from $2.80 to almost $4.20. Ground beef, once a Tuesday evening staple, was switched out for a one-time treat each week, rather than the five days we would typically enjoy, in favor of lentils and canned beans that my father purchased in bulk from a Sam's Club membership he had previously refused to obtain for years.

My then 12-year-old younger brother would no longer get individual snack packs (his favorite) to bring to school for lunch as their individual price had nearly doubled. We'd even plant a small garden that spring with tomatoes, peppers, and zucchini - not as a fun hobby, but because the cost of produce had increased almost 8% just for the year.

It's unethical to advertise to kids under 12 because children often don't understand the difference between persuasion and information. The American Academy of Pediatrics reported in 2020 that kids under age 8 typically struggle to understand the intent behind ads. This puts them at particular risk of seeing ads for sugary cereals, toys, games, or fast food. For instance, a 6-year-old might think a cartoon character selling a colorful cereal is just telling them about a fun product to try, without realizing it's a company's paid pitch to boost sales.

This is especially problematic when ads use personal information or digital media. In 2019, Google settled for $170 million with the FTC and NY Attorney General after they were accused of illegally gathering kids' data on YouTube without sufficient parental consent. And even without data collection, online games blur the lines between ads and play. A kid might miss the fact that some in-game rewards, influencer content, or "unboxing" campaigns are trying to get them to buy something.

That's not to say all kid-targeted ads need to be outlawed. Ads can also lead to books, educational shows, sports gear, or healthy foods. And companies need ads to provide jobs and competition. But ethics matter because kids lack adult experience, independence, and critical thinking skills. It's wrong for companies to exploit them with manipulations, undisclosed endorsements, false health messages, or peer pressure to convince their parents. Also, it's unethical for them to harvest kids' data for targeted ads.

Parents play a role, but it's unfair to leave it to them alone while companies use armies of psychologists, designers, and data scientists to sway kids. We need rules that ban targeted ads for under-12s, demand transparent disclosures for sponsored media, limit unhealthy food ads on kid shows, and have severe punishments. Not to take kids' agency away, but to help them grow into it. Ethics in advertising means recognizing childhood as an era of education and development, not just an arena for exploiting young consumers.

Given that children under 12 lack the sophistication to tell persuasion from information, advertising to them poses major ethical issues. For instance, a 6-year-old might think a cartoon character endorsing a colorful cereal just suggests a fun product, unaware that the company paid to push its sales.

When advertising goes online or utilizes data, the ethical concerns deepen. Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884) reaches the critical moment in Huck's moral development late in the book, when he must decide whether to write Miss Watson, informing her of Jim's (her run away slave's) whereabouts or whether to "go to hell" and destroy the letter. As Huck pens his message to Jim's owner in St. Petersburg (of Hannibal fame) he feels "washed clean of sin." Until he thinks of all the 1,000 miles he's floated down the Mississippi, Cairo's fog, and Jim calling him "honey" and acting as a father towards him. Clutching the note, Huck trembles, recalls his brief prayer. And finally says, "All right, then, I'll go to hell." And he rips the paper in two.

The scene is important for what it reveals about Huck; his conscience has been destroyed by society not by his own depravity. His Sunday school lessons and lessons from Widow Douglas have instructed him that helping a slave run away is stealing and damned. "Doing the right thing" in his world means to betray his friend. And in true irony, Twain has Huck identify as a sinner just when he's acting most morally. In opting to go to hell rather than Jim to re-slavery, Huck is not just denying Miss Watson's ownership. He's also opting out of an entire system of values. The moral progress Huck makes is in learning to rely on the "sound heart" of his own experience rather than the "deformed conscience" of his society (a term Twain himself wrote in a notebook in 1895 to explain the central issue in the book).

The turning point is also a victory of empathy over abstract moral law. Huck can't think his way to abolitionism. He's not philosophically inclined in that regard. Rather he has the memories: Jim crying over his daughter 'Lizabeth that he swatted before he realized she was deaf; Jim's joy at seeing Huck after the feud with the Grangerfords; both of them fighting like a family on the raft over King Solomon and the Frenchmen. Huck's morality comes from the sum of human experiences. It's not a matter of ideology.

We can see that in the novel's conclusion where Tom Sawyer reduces Jim's already free status to a game. It undoes Huck's progression. Not completely though. When Huck elects hell, Twain is suggesting that conscience isn't a fixed moral lodestone given by society. It's something you have to create yourself, through decisions built upon loyalty and affection. Huck doesn't become a respectable person. He becomes a good person.

At the conclusion of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), Huck's crucial moral test arrives: should he write to Miss Watson telling her the whereabouts of her runaway slave Jim or go to "hell" and destroy the letter. "Washed clean of sin," Huck thinks when he jots down the message to Jim's owner in St. Petersburg (set in Hannibal). But he recalls the one thousand miles they've floated on the Mississippi. The fog at Cairo. Jim calling him "honey," treating him like a father. Huck holds the letter. He shakes, remembers his short prayer. "All right, then," he says. "I'll go to hell." He crumples the note into two pieces.

Why is this so significant? Because Huck's conscience isn't shattered by his own sinfulness. It's shattered by his society. He's learned from his Sunday school, his Widow Douglas, that helping a slave escape is stealing and sinning. Doing "the right thing" here means betraying his friend. Twain's irony stings: Huck thinks he's a sinner at the very moment he's behaving most morally. In opting for hell rather than having Jim re-enslaved, Huck is rejecting not just Miss Watson's ownership but a whole system of values. He's growing in morality by recognizing he must follow the "sound heart" of his experiences rather than the "deformed conscience" of his culture. (The last term is one Twain actually used in a notebook from 1895 to describe the central issue in the novel.)

It's also a victory of empathy over theory. Huck can't intellectualize his way to abolition. He isn't a political philosopher. He has memories. He remembers Jim crying over his daughter 'Lizabeth (before he punched her not knowing she was deaf). Jim's joy at seeing Huck alive after his spat with the Grangerfords. Their quarrels on the raft about King Solomon and Frenchmen, like family. Huck's ethics grow out of hours and days of shared humanity.

The novel's ending (with Tom Sawyer turning Jim's already-granted freedom into a game) is rightly criticized for diluting Huck's progress. But it can't undo it. When Huck opts for hell, Twain suggests conscience isn't a god-given compass you're handed by society. It's something you must construct through acts of loyalty and love, bit by bit. Huck doesn't become respectable. He becomes good.
