Between 1849 and (roughly) 1860, Harriet Tubman undertook roughly 13 trips back into the slave-holding South. All of them were in direct violation of federal law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made it a crime not only to run away from slavery, but to aid someone else in doing so. The law levied fines up to $1,000 and prison sentences on abettors, prevented accused fugitives from having a jury trial, and required all citizens in the North to help with arrests when called upon. Tubman, having escaped slavery herself from Dorchester County, Maryland in 1849, responded to this law by returning to the very place it was meant to enforce. 
 Tubman's approach subverted the very machinery of the Fugitive Slave Act. She travelled at night, frequently in the winter, when patrols would be weaker and darkness longer, navigating her way by the North Star and by word-of-mouth contacts with others on the so-called Underground Railroad, leading people northward. And following the 1850 law's penetration into the free states, even Philadelphia and New York were no longer safe places for her to bring people, so Tubman expanded her trips north to St. Catharines, Ontario in Canada, where people were outside of the jurisdiction of U.S. marshals under the laws of the British Empire. In all, Tubman is thought to have personally led around 70 enslaved people to freedom, including her own family, all of this despite the fact that a rumored $40,000 bounty was said to be on her head for capture. 
 The reasons why these trips were direct violations of the Fugitive Slave Act, as opposed to simple escapes, was because she kept coming back. Where the Act assumed that the fear of it would cause people to lock the border down, Tubman not only crossed it frequently, but in the most dangerous direction, in order to liberate other people. In addition, she famously armed herself with a pistol, for protection and, according to later stories, for forcing forward anyone who panicked and became fearful of running away and giving away the group. During the Civil War, she took this direct defiance even further by acting as a scout/spy for the Union Army, and helping lead the 1863 Combahee River raid in South Carolina which liberated more than 700 enslaved people in a single night. 
 Tubman's 13 missions prove that, for all its brutality on paper, the Fugitive Slave Act was no match for someone willing to accept the penalties as the cost of the work, rather than as a disincentive.

Tubman's 13 trips back into the South between 1849 and 1860, so to speak, were direct violations of federal law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made it not only illegal to escape slavery, but to aid anyone else in escaping. It called for up to a $1,000 fine and jail time for those aiding others in escaping, did not grant alleged fugitive slaves the right to a jury trial, and required all free citizens in the North to actively aid in their capture if asked to. Tubman, having escaped slavery herself in 1849 from Dorchester County, MD, responded to this Act by travelling back into the very area it sought to control. 
 Tubman used the Act itself against itself. She would often travel at night, particularly during winter when the patrols were more sparse and the days were shorter. She used the North Star and mouth-to-mouth information of the Underground Railroad to transport people northward. After the passing of the 1850 Act, the extension of its power into the free states meant that cities such as Philadelphia or even New York were not safe destinations. So Tubman widened her routes to St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada where escapees were protected from U.S. Marshals under British law. She personally claimed to have led about 70 slaves to freedom, including her own family, and all of this she did while the rumor of a $40,000 bounty on her capture circulated. 
 And this is what made her missions direct acts of defiance of the Act. It wasn't just escape, it was constant going back. The Act assumed that fear would act as a one-way border. Tubman would not only cross it, but she would cross it in the most dangerous direction, to bring people out. She was armed with a pistol, not only for her own defense but also, according to later reports, to push those who got scared and wanted to go back and blow their cover. During the Civil War, she would further push her defiance by acting as a scout and spy for the Union Army, and even leading part of the raid on the Combahee River in 1863 in South Carolina, freeing more than 700 slaves in one night. 
 Tubman's 13 missions reveal the weakness of the Fugitive Slave Act in the face of someone who could live with its consequences as the price of the work to be done, not as a deterrent.

For Kant, ethics is governed by universal laws. You can't calculate outcomes. A lie could unexpectedly lead to adverse consequences, and it erodes our faith in the veracity of others' promises. Yet, this example doesn't guarantee that any lie told for protective purposes is ethical. One could say, "I'm lying for your own good," but be driven by a motive such as wanting to avoid embarrassment, save time, or exert control. Thus, a lie is only excusable if the danger is imminent, the damage is grave, there is no other truthful option, and the individual lying is accountable for the outcome. Though Kant's rule is absolute and essential for maintaining trust, the lifeguard's dilemma reminds us that ethics must account for our frailty. So the short answer is yes. Six weeks out from ACL reconstruction it's very normal to have aches and pains but it really depends on WHAT type of soreness. 
 
 I'm four months out from my hamstring ACL reconstruction (done at Johns Hopkins on Feb 14) and at 6 weeks out I was still experiencing general aching everyday, especially around my incision sites and where the hamstring tendon was harvested (inside my knee). My PT explained that this is normal because at 6 weeks that's when the graft is in it's most weak stage of healing ("ligamentization" stage). And you're probably increasing activity--more walking, stationary bike, possibly leg presses--stressing the graft in different ways. 
 
 Normal at 6 weeks: 
 General soreness after PT sessions/long days on feet 
 Soreness in portal incisions and donor site 
 Some stiffness if you sit in one position too long 
 Mild swelling that resolves overnight 
 
 Not normal/time to call your surgeon 
 - Sharp/sudden pain (especially with a pivot) 
 - New notable swelling that doesn't resolve with ice and elevation 
 - Warmth, redness, fever (infection, call don't wait on this!) 
 - Knee instability or the feeling that your knee is "giving out" 
 - Calf pain (could be a blood clot) 
 
  My surgeon's advice was that as a general rule you should be feeling a slow improvement from week to week, even if you have some day to day fluctuation. But if you're not experiencing improvement in your soreness and it's stable or worsening over a two week period, call and have it checked out. 
 
 Things that helped for me--15-20 minute icing after every PT session, continuing my quad sets and heel slides (even when sore, movement helps), using a pillow under my knee for sleeping. And make sure you're not limping. The compensating with your hip can also cause soreness that can be mistaken for knee soreness. 
 
 With all of that said I'm just some random dude on the internet. NOT your surgeon. Call their office if something doesn't feel right. Most have a nurse line and they'd rather answer a "silly" question than you have some complication. It's still relatively early. Most people don't really start feeling "good" until 3-4 months. You're still 6 weeks out.

tl;dr - yes, it's normal to have soreness at 6 weeks after ACL reconstruction.  But not all soreness is created equal.

Soreness (dull ache) after PT or being on your feet a lot
 soreness in areas of portal incision or donor site
soreness from sitting in one position too long
slight swelling that resolves overnight
 NOT normal, call your surgeon:

warms, red, fever (possibly infection - don't screw around)
feeling instability in your knee/your knee "gives way"
pain in calf (possibility of blood clot) 
Per my surgeon, you should be seeing things getting gradually better from week to week (although day-to-day it may be varied).  If your soreness is not improving or is getting worse over 2 weeks call them.

The key is oven or better yet toaster oven/air fryer. Microwaving makes crust soggy and rubbery like cardboard (heating only moisture content of breading). 
 
 The way to do it is 
 1) bring it to room temp (20-30min) before heating 
 If you heat cold chicken to hot from fridge, it doesn't heat evenly and you will overcook outside to try to warm inside. 
 
 2) Heat oven to 400F (200C) 
 Put wire rack on a sheet pan. (MOST IMPORTANT STEP PEOPLE MISS) 
 The air flowing underneath prevents the bottom from steaming and getting soggy like it will if you just put the pieces on the sheet pan 
 
 3) 15-20min for bone-in, 10-12min for boneless/tenders. 
 Flip halfway 
 Cook to 165F (74C) internal temp. Use instant read thermometer at thickest part near bone. 
 
 4) Don't use foil or cover. 
 That traps the steam and ruins the whole process. 
 
 If you have an air fryer, its even quicker and may even be crisper. 
 375F (190C) 4-6min. Don't have to flip. It'll circulate air all around. 
 I've done this with leftover KFC style thighs and Popeye's tenders and they were almost as crispy as fresh. 
 
 As a final step to help if you feel crust is a bit soft after heating, you can broil for last 60-90seconds while watching closely not to burn. 
 It'll crisp up any area that the convection oven didn't. 
 
 Don't microwave at all unless you really don't care about crust. 30sec will noticeably soften it.

The oven (or toaster/airfryer) wins every time. Micro makes it rubbery cardboard because it's just heating the moisture inside the breading. 
 What you want to do is: 
 1. Bring it to room temperature (20-30 mins) before reheating. Cold-to-hot fridgerated/refrigerated cooking causes uneven reheating and you overcook the outside to try to get the inside warm 
 2. Pre-heat oven to 400F (200C).  Place a wire rack on a sheet pan. This is the crucial step people miss. You need the air circulation under the chicken to avoid steaming and turning soggy (which happens if you just place the pieces on the pan). 
 3. For bone-in pieces, 15-20 mins. For boneless/tenders, 10-12 mins (400F / 200C).  Flip once.  Internal temp should be 165F (74C). Test with instant read thermometer in the thickest part near the bone 
 4. Don't use foil or cover it up. This will cause steaming and ruin the effect. 
 
 If you have air fryer, it's even quicker and probably more crispy.  375F (190C) for 4-6 mins. Don't need to flip because there's air circulation all around. I've done this with leftover KFC style thighs and Popeye's tenders. It's almost as crispy as fresh. 
 
 If the breading feels a bit soft even after reheating, you can try the final step. Place it under the broiler for the last 60-90 seconds and watch it carefully to avoid burning. Direct heat will crisp up areas that weren't completely done by convection. 
 
 Don't use microwave unless you don't care about the breading. Even 30 seconds will noticeably soften it.

Don't try to make Git handle conflicts, try to minimize the number of lines being changed by two different people.

For example, in our checkout-web repo, Maya is in charge of the layout of `CartSummary.jsx` and Jordan is in charge of the tax calculation hook. We split the component into several files.

```text
CartSummary/
  CartSummary.jsx
  useCartTotals.js
  CartLineItem.jsx
  CartSummary.test.jsx
```

Maya and Jordan each create short-lived branches (like `maya/cart-layout` or `jordan/tax-hook`). They branch off `main` just before they begin. We create pull requests within a day or two, rather than letting branches live for weeks. We run this before we create the PR:

```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
npm test -- CartSummary
```

Also, supply the component with data from props, rather than letting many developers change the same internal code. For example, let `CartSummary.jsx` display `subtotal`, `tax`, and `total`. Let `useCartTotals.js` handle the calculation. This way, Jordan can alter the calculations without disturbing Maya's JSX.

If you really have to change the same lines of code, at least coordinate the order in which you will integrate the changes. Suppose it's September 21, 2026. Maya will merge her structural refactor. Then Jordan can rebase off of that and adjust the interface of the hook. Don't resolve the conflict from each of your branches.

Keep commits small and narrow. It's so much easier to read/rebase a commit like `Extract CartLineItem` than one that has some formatting, some dependency updates, some business logic. Turn on branch protection and enforce passing CI before they can merge. That way, the second PR is run against the latest `main` before it gets merged.

Any dense banana bread with a clean skewer is a sign of both over-moisture and not baking long enough. The toothpick test is pretty terrible in this case. Bananas are insanely wet. They'll create a super wet batter that can remain gumminess/compressed even once the starches have gelled enough that it won't stick to the skewer. Here's what I would try: 
 1) You probably have an oven temp issue. Get an oven thermometer (Target, $8?). My old GE was 25F too cold which baked the edges much longer than the interior. This is a very common cause of the inside being dense. 
 2) Internal temp is more reliable than skewer. Banana bread is done at 200-205F in the middle. I use Thermapen, but any instant read thermometer. If you take it out at 200F, it will finish properly via carry over. 
 3) You probably are using too much banana. Most recipes are looking for ~1C mashed (so, like 3 med bananas ~240g). If you're putting in 5 extra large bananas because they're "going bad" you may have added an extra 1/2C liquid. The excess banana won't evaporate, it will just be gumminess. Freeze the extra banana instead. 
 4) Baking soda test. Baking soda has a shelf life. If yours is from 2023 and has been open, replace it. Put some in hot water. If there's not a lot of enthusiastic fizz, toss it. 
 5) Try baking it lower temp/longer. E.g. 325F instead of 350F for 60-75min in 9x5 pan. Baking slower can allow the center to catch up. You can tent the top with foil at 45min if browning quickly. 
 6) Don't over-mix. Stir/mix until flour is no longer visible. Gluten is what makes it chewy and dense. 
 7) Allow it to cool completely in the pan (~1hr). Warm banana bread slices can make the center appear denser/wetter than it really is. 
 
 I would guess that if I could only get you to do one thing, it would be get a thermometer and bake it to 200-205F. That's what solved this for me (after 2 years of dense bread!)

 2. Internal temperature better than toothpick. Banana bread wants to be 200-205°F in the middle when done. I have a Thermapen but any IR thermometer works. If you take it out when it's 200°F, it'll have perfect carryover baking.

This is due to the fact that numbers in javascript are stored as IEEE 754 doubles, and 0.1 and 0.2 are not exactly representable as binary floats (they're converted to the closest approximate value). 0.1 is actually represented as something like 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827, 0.2 is like 0.200000000000000011102230246251565. Adding them and converting to the closest double (rounding) gives 0.30000000000000004 (not 0.3). This isn't just a javascript problem - this happens in python, java, c, any language which uses standard floating point numbers (ie per IEEE 754). Just try to do 0.1 + 0.2 in Node.js or the console of your browser. It will be obvious.

When it comes to money you should avoid using raw floats to do calculations that you want to sum or compare exactly. Some good alternatives:

1. Use integer cents/minor units - for 19.99 you would represent it as an integer - 1999, and then do calculations using integers, and only divide by 100 for display purposes. This is the simplest approach and will work fine until you need fractional cents or very large amounts.
2. Use a decimal library - decimal.js or big.js or bignumber.js. They represent numbers as base 10 decimals, not binary floats so 0.1 + 0.2 will = 0.3. E.g. new Decimal('0.1').plus('0.2').toString() will give you "0.3"
3. If you don't need decimals in the middle of calculations, use the native BigInt and do integer calculations in whole cents. BigInts don't have this kind of float precision problems with large integers
4. In newer systems be aware of problems with Number.prototype.toFixed - toFixed doesn't solve the underlying precision problem, it just rounds the string used for display. So don't use it for actual calculations - just formatting.

Basically: use floats for measurements and graphics. Use integers or decimal libraries for money.

This is because Javascript uses IEEE 754 double precision floats which means that 0.1 and 0.2 are not exact and therefore stored as the closest approximation. 0.1 is actually stored as ~0.1000000000000000055511151231257827 and 0.2 as ~0.200000000000000011102230246251565. When you add them and round to the closest representable double, it's not 0.3, it's 0.30000000000000004. It's not a javascript bug, it's the same in python, java, c, and any other language that implements the usual floating point math (i.e. IEEE 754). Just type 0.1 + 0.2 into a console in Node.js or your browser dev tools, and you'll see it right away.

For money, you definitely should not just use raw floats for calculations that you will be comparing and/or summing up. You should:

1. use integers for cents/minor units, so for example $19.99 is stored as 1999 (an integer), and you use integers for your calculations, and then only divide by 100 for output. this is the easiest solution and works well as long as you don't need fractional cents or massive sums

2. use some sort of decimal library. e.g. decimal.js, big.js, bignumber.js. these libraries store numbers as base-10 decimals (rather than binary floats) so that 0.1 + 0.2 does indeed equal 0.3. so for example you can do new Decimal('0.1').plus('0.2').toString() and it'll return "0.3"

3. use native bigints for whole-cent integer math if you don't need any actual decimals in calculations. BigInt is great in that it doesn't suffer from the float precision issues for large integers.

4. Also be aware of the new Number.prototype.toFixed issues if you're using more recent environments -- toFixed doesn't actually solve the problem of precision, it only affects the output string that it's rounding, so don't use it to do actual calculations. Only use it for displaying.

Generally speaking, use floats for measuring and graphics, use integers (or decimal libraries) for money.

So if you've got, say $42k in federal direct loans and are on track for 120 qualifying payments - generally speaking you should just make the qualifying IDR payments and otherwise invest your extra, instead of prepaying for forgiveness voluntarily. This is actually the intended functionality. 
 A normal 15amp circuit in your house rated at 120v has a maximum capacity of 1800w.  However, the national electrical code stipulates that you shouldn't load a circuit continuously at more than 80% of its capacity.  So, you can only use 1440w or so safely. 
 Your Microwave is probably 1000-1500w (1200W microwave really consumes 1500w or so at the wall because its not 100% efficient) 
 Your toaster is probably 800-1500w (common 2 slice is 900-1200w or so) 
 So now you are using a 1200w microwave and a 1000w toaster, that's ~2200w, which is more than your max of 1800w.  Therefore, the breaker is popping because its doing its job!  Protecting the wires from getting too hot. 
 
 What can you do? 
 
 1.  Don't use them at the same time.  Toast first, then microwave.  Pain but free. 
 2.  Move one to a different circuit.  In most kitchens after mid 90's, you should have at least two 20amp small appliance circuits at the counter tops for code requirements.  If you have one single 15amp circuit for everything, that's a flag that you have really old wiring that's not up to modern code.  Try plugging the toaster into a different wall (it may be on a different circuit breaker).  You can test this by plugging lamps in to each outlet and cycling breakers off one at a time to figure out which outlet is on which. 
 3.  Upgrade.  If you only have a single 15amp circuit for your kitchen, the cost of an electrician adding a 20amp small appliance circuit is probably $300-$600 and worth doing if you cook a lot. 
 
 Don't do this:  Don't change the breaker from 15amp to 20amp.  Circuit breakers are rated to protect the wire they are connected to.  15amp breakers protect 14gauge wire.  If you upsize the breaker, it might let the wire overheat without tripping in the wall without you knowing.  This is the cause of electrical fires. 
 
 TL;DR:  Microwave and toaster add up to more power than your circuit can handle.  The breaker is not broken.  Its saving your house.

 -Unplug one and plug it into another circuit. 
 Most kitchens built since the mid-1990s are actually required to have 2 minimum "small appliance" 20amp circuits at the counter per the code. 
 If your kitchen only has a single 15amp circuit doing all the things, that's an indication that your kitchen is probably wired before modern code. 
 Try unplugging the toaster and moving it to another wall. Maybe it's on a separate circuit! 
 You can test this by plugging in a lamp to each outlet and turning breakers off to determine which outlets each breaker turns off. 
 -Upgrades! 
 If you have a single 15amp circuit for your kitchen, it's usually $300-$600 to have an electrician install a 20amp "small appliance" circuit. If you cook a lot it's probably worth it. 
 **Things you should NOT do** 
 DO NOT replace the 15amp circuit breaker with a 20amp one! 
 The circuit breaker is chosen to protect the size of the wire. 
 15amp breakers protect 14 gauge wire. 
 Using a larger circuit breaker could cause that wire to overheat in your walls without triggering the circuit breaker! 
 It's how electrical fires happen. 
 TL:DR 
 Microwave + Toaster are drawing too much. 
 Circuit breaker is not broken. 
 It's saving your house.

Ibuprofen + acetaminophen combination is safe, yes. In fact, it's a common (and well-studied) way to treat migraine headaches. Ibuprofen and acetaminophen have different mechanisms of action (ibuprofen is an NSAID that decreases inflammation, acetaminophen mechanism is still disputed but it is more of a central action), so they don't work in the same pathway and can be used together. 
 A common dose for an average adult (no contraindications) would be 400mg ibuprofen + 500-1000mg acetaminophen to be used together at the beginning of the migraine symptoms.  
 Some over the counter combined medications (Excedrin migraine for example - 250mg acetaminophen + 250mg aspirin + 65mg caffeine) are designed on this "multiple mechanisms of action" principle. But in this case, aspirin is used, not ibuprofen. 
 
 Max daily dose of acetaminophen is 3000-4000mg for an average healthy adult (nowadays many clinicians advise not to exceed 3000mg/day if taken regularly). 500mg in one dose is far from the max, even if you will repeat the dose in 6-8h. 
 Max daily dose for ibuprofen OTC is usually 1200mg/day (400mg every 6h). But a doctor can prescribe up to 3200mg/day (in some cases). 
 Be careful if you plan to use a 3rd product: many "migraine" or "sinus" combined pills use acetaminophen, and it is easy to go above max daily dose of acetaminophen when combining. 
 Be careful if you have liver disease or heavy alcohol use (acetaminophen); or kidney disease, stomach ulcers, GERD, and/or taking anticoagulants like warfarin (ibuprofen). If you're pregnant, or above 65, or use other medications daily - check this with pharmacist at your local pharmacy (it's a 2min question and you can get a check if this particular combination may affect your other medications). 
 If you have migraines frequently and using these combination more than 2-3 times per week - then it's better to seek a treatment from a doctor (preventive treatment) instead of OTC combinations (too frequent use can also lead to medication overuse headache).

 - Typical max OTC dose Ibuprofen a day is 1200mg (400mg every 6hrs). Doctor may prescribe up to 3200mg a day.

MEMORANDUM

TO: Maria Kowalski, CEO; Jan Freitag, CTO
FROM: Elena Rasmussen, Data Protection Officer
DATE: 12 May 2025
RE: GDPR Data Retention Compliance: Expansion of Kowalski Customer Database in EU

PURPOSE: This memo outlines our GDPR data retention requirements and pre-launch steps to support our upcoming Kowalski customer database expansion into new EU markets (Germany, Netherlands, Poland) as of 1 September 2025.

KEY REQUIREMENTS:
1. DATA RETENTION PERIODS (Art. 5(1)(e)): Data must not be retained beyond the period necessary. Our current practice of indefinite retention of inactive customer data is not compliant. Draft plan: Transactional data: 7 years (Polish and German tax requirements); Marketing data/consent: Consent period + 3 years for audit trail; Abandoned cart browsing: max 90 days.

2. AUTOMATED RETENTION DELETION: Engineering (P. Nowak's team) must establish automated deletion/anonymisation processes in CRM by 15 Aug 2025 (quarterly manual deletions inadequate - anticipating 2.4m new EU data records).

3. DATA MINIMISATION AT MIGRATION: Only data fields required for order fulfilment and compliance should be migrated. Legacy data (e.g. ID scan retention for fraud purposes 2016-19) must be deleted before migration, not after.

4. PROCESSING RECORDS (Art. 30): Retention schedule must be incorporated into our processing register - to be reviewed by our supervisory authority (probably Polish UODO, as our Warsaw office will be main establishment for EU processing).

5. DATA SUBJECT RIGHTS: Privacy notices and data subject access/erasure responses should reflect retention schedules. Exceptions exist for legal holds (e.g. potential litigation Bergmann Logistics) - these must be documented.

RISKS: Inadequate retention carries risk of fines to max €20m or 4% global turnover and affects our legitimacy for marketing (Art. 6(1)(a)).

ACTIONS/OWNERS:

ACTION OWNER DEADLINE
Approve data retention schedule Executive Committee 30 May 2025
Delete legacy ID scans IT Ops (L. Hansen) 20 June 2025
Establish automated retention deletion Engineering (P. Nowak) 15 Aug 2025
Revise privacy notices/Art. 30 DPO office 22 Aug 2025

Will seek 30 min leadership meeting on 28 May to finalise retention schedule. Cost impact €85k for tools/external review (included in FY2025 compliance budget).

To: Executive Leadership Team From: Finance & Strategy Date: September 21, 2026 Subject: Q2 FY26 Financial Performance Summary

Q2 FY26 consolidated sales increased 7.1% year-on-year to $412.6 million (from $385.2 million in Q2 FY25), supported by solid growth in Medical Devices (+11.4%) and Consumer Diagnostics (+9.2%). Nonetheless, Pharmaceutical division gross margin declined sharply to 38.4% (from 44.9% in Q2 FY25), resulting in a 650 bps margin decline and partially offsetting otherwise robust top-line growth - ultimately reducing consolidated operating margin to 19.8% from 22.3%.

The primary drivers of pharma margin pressure include: (1) a 14% increase in costs of goods sold (COGS) for active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) from our Hyderabad and Cork manufacturing plants (due to supply chain issues in March/April); (2) early generic substitution driven by loss of patent protection for Nexovant (our second-largest branded product by sales) in January (causing average sales price to decline by ~18% in the U.S. market sooner than anticipated); (3) non-recurring inventory write-offs ($6.2 million) in May for obsolete inventory at our Raleigh manufacturing facility.

With pharmaceutical sales largely flat ($148.3 million; +0.6% YoY), the pharma business disproportionately weighed on consolidated cost structure without meaningfully contributing to overall revenue growth. At current run-rates, we expect the full-year pharma gross margin to approach ~39% (versus -500 bps to FY25 gross margin of 44.1%).

Q3 recommended actions: (1) accelerate API dual-sourcing with our Basel supplier to mitigate future input costs volatility by year-end; (2) prioritize Nexovant-XR reformulation and aim for FDA submission by November 15 to partially re-establish branded price premium; (3) finalize process review at Raleigh by October 10 to avoid further inventory write-offs.

We'll provide the Board with an in-depth pharma margin recovery plan at our October 14 meeting.

9/21/2026 62% of our rare earth elements are coming from our single supplier in Shenzhen, China, Shenzhen Huanyu Materials Co. The high dependency poses a supply chain risk to our material supply for products being built in our San Jose, CA facility, especially for components with NDD (Neodymium, Dysprosium, Terbium) for motors and HEPMAGs (high efficiency magnets).

The biggest risk is single-point supplier failure due to export restriction, port issues, power outage, quality issue, labor shortage, geopolitical situation, and financial. The delay of about 18K finished units during the single point failure for 30 days may involve premium freight, accelerated qualification, or rescheduling. We currently have about 7 weeks of inventory stock but this may not be enough for long-term interruption or when the demand surges at the same time.

This needs to be considered a top management concern as an operation and compliance risk. By the end of 12/31/2026, Procurement should have at least two more suppliers (one in Vietnam/Malaysia and one in Mexico/US) to be qualified. The goal is to drop Shenzhen supplier's dependency to be less than 40% by 6/30/2027 and less than 25% by 12/31/2027. Engineering/Quality should work on the 2nd source on material composition, magnetic properties, reliability, change control etc., before the volume migration.

Finance should be prepared for the risk reserve on fast shipping and alternative materials until the alternatives are qualified. Legal/Compliance should check on applicable export regulation, forced labor, sanction check, and supply chain disclosure from US for this. Also ask procurement to put 90 days safety stock assurance, business continuity, notification requirement on change of production, ownership, regulation etc.

COO should have a monthly dashboard on supplier allocation, weeks of inventory on-hand, qualification status, corrective action in-hand, country of origin etc. While the situation is manageable, it needs clear targets to be reduced, management attention, and funded resource for alternative suppliers.

Summary As of September 21, 2026, 62% of our rare earth elements come from a single vendor in Shenzhen, China Shenzhen Huanyu Materials Co. This poses a significant risk in our material supply chain for goods manufactured at our San Jose, CA plant, specifically those materials with neodymium, dysprosium and terbium used in motors and high efficiency magnets.

The risk relates to single point of failure with the vendor for any reason (e.g., export, ports, power outages, defects, labor shortages, geopolitical, and/or financial). A disruption of 30 days can cause a delay of 18k finished units and could require premium freight/expedite qualification or production changes. We have about 7 weeks of inventory as of today, but this may not be enough in case of long-term disruption or the coincidence with higher demand.

It is crucial for the management to address this concentration as a very urgent risk for both operations and compliance. By December 31, 2026, we should have at least 2 approved alternative suppliers, 1 in VN or MY and 1 in MX or US. The goal is to achieve less than 40% from Shenzhen vendor by June 30, 2027 and less than 25% by December 31, 2027. It is important that Engineering and Quality establish second sourcing (material composition, magnetic, reliability and engineering change documentation) before we make changes to the volume.

In the meantime, we should establish risk reserve from Finance to cover urgent logistics and alternative materials and work with Legal and Compliance on US export restrictions, forced labor, sanctions, supply chain disclosure, etc. Procurement should work on securing a 90-days safety stock, business continuity, notification of production changes, ownership and regulatory changes, etc.

COO should be provided with a monthly dashboard with supplier allocation, weeks on hand, qualification statuses, open corrective actions and country of origin exposure. This risk is not necessarily unmanageable, but we need clear targets of reduction, executive support, and investments in second sources.

Abstract
The hepatic uptake transporter, OATP1B1 (SLCO1B1) is involved in the hepatic uptake of many endogenous substrates and clinically relevant drugs such as statins. Gain of systemic exposure to statins and risk of myopathy is observed with common loss-of-function *SLCO1B1* alleles such as the rs4149056 T>C polymorphism (c.521T>C, Val174Ala). The relative contribution of OATP1B1 to the total hepatocellular uptake of specific substrates is, however, not fully understood. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-Cas9-based SLCO1B1 knockout in HepG2 cells to directly quantify the contribution of the transporter to hepatic uptake. We used two single guide RNAs in exon 2 and 6 of SLCO1B1 to create clonal knockouts that were validated by Sanger sequencing, RT-qPCR showing >95% decrease in SLCO1B1 transcript level, and Western blot showing no OATP1B1 protein. Off-target analysis of the whole genome for the top 10 predicted off-target sites by targeted amplicon sequencing identified no indels greater than 1.2% allele frequency. When uptake was measured at 37°C for 5 min using fluorescent pravastatin (10 µM), uptake was reduced by 43.0% ± 3.8% (mean ± SEM, *n* = 4 independent experiments, *p* < 0.001, two-tailed unpaired *t*-test) in the knockout clones compared to wild-type HepG2 cells and non-targeting guide RNA. This residual uptake was not sensitive to the OATP inhibitor, rifampicin (100 µM), but was partially inhibited by probenecid, indicating that it may involve other organic anion transporters, likely including OATP1B3 and Na⁺-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide, which remained expressed in the knockout clones. Kinetic analysis suggested that the decrease in uptake was due to a 46% decrease in maximal transport capacity (Vmax: 285 ± 31 vs. 528 ± 44 pmol/mg protein/5 min) with no significant alteration in apparent Km. Thus, we have provided a direct quantitative measurement of the contribution of OATP1B1 to statin uptake in a human hepatocyte model and developed a validated isogenic knockout system that can be used for substrate- and genotype-dependent drug disposition screening for precision dosing of OATP1B1 substrates in carriers of loss-of-function alleles.

Abstract
The hepatic uptake transporter encoded by the solute carrier organic anion transporter family 1B member 1 (OATP1B1, SLCO1B1) is responsible for the uptake of many endogenous molecules and clinically relevant drugs such as statins, into hepatocytes. Although common loss-of-function variants in SLCO1B1, like the rs4149056 T>C polymorphism (c.521T>C, Val174Ala), are known to cause higher systemic statin levels and an increased risk of statin-associated myopathy, the exact quantitative relevance of OATP1B1 for total hepatocellular uptake of specific substrates is unclear. To directly measure the extent of the involvement of OATP1B1 in hepatic uptake, we developed a CRISPR-Cas9-induced knockout of SLCO1B1 in HepG2 cells. We created SLCO1B1 knockout cell lines via CRISPR-Cas9 using two single guide RNAs targeting exons 2 and 6 of SLCO1B1. Clonal knockout cell lines were verified by Sanger sequencing, RT-qPCR showing >95% decrease in SLCO1B1 mRNA levels, and the lack of OATP1B1 protein expression by Western blot. We determined that there were no indels present with a frequency above 1.2% by off-target assessment of the whole genome with targeted amplicon sequencing at the 10 predicted off-target loci. We measured an uptake decrease of 43.0% ± 3.8% (mean ± SEM, *n* = 4 independent experiments, *p* < 0.001, 2-tailed unpaired *t*-test) for knockout clones compared to wild-type HepG2 cells and non-targeting guide RNA control cells at 37°C within 5 min, when we used fluorescently labeled pravastatin (10 µM) for uptake. No effect of the OATP inhibitor rifampicin (100 µM) was observed for the remaining uptake, whereas the uptake was partially reduced by probenecid. This suggests a role of other organic anion transporters, potentially OATP1B3 and Na⁺-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide, for the remaining uptake. These two transporters were still present in the knockout clones. The uptake decrease was due to a decrease in maximal transport capacity (Vmax) of 46% (285 ± 31 pmol/mg protein/5 min vs 528 ± 44 pmol/mg protein/5 min) without a significant alteration of apparent Km. We now provide direct quantitative data about the role of OATP1B1 in statin uptake in a human hepatocyte model. Furthermore, we present a validated isogenic knockout approach that can be used to screen for substrate-and genotype-dependent effects of drug disposition and has consequences for the precision dosing of OATP1B1 substrate drugs for loss-of-function allele carriers.

Methods
A total of 240 veterans (M age = 47.3 y, SD = 12.1 y, 68% male) were enrolled from March 2021 through November 2022 (mean = 47.3 years old, SD = 12.1 years, 68% male) from outpatient services within the VA Puget Sound Health Care System (Seattle, WA) and the VA Boston Healthcare System (Boston, MA). Individuals were eligible if they met DSM-5 criteria for chronic insomnia disorder and had a score ≥15 on the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and no active suicidal ideation or untreated psychosis. Comorbid PTSD (n = 142, 59%) was included to be representative of the intended population. Of 412 individuals referred, 240 were randomized 1:1 using a computergenerated permuted block design (block size = 4, stratified by location and PTSD status) to receive cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I, n = 120) or an active control intervention (sleep hygiene education with attentionmatched contact, n = 120).

CBT-I was provided in six 50-minute individual sessions over 7 weeks by 14 doctoral-level psychologists, who were trained to a criterion fidelity rating of ≥90% on a standardized fidelity checklist and incorporated sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, and relapse prevention. Control group members received a single 30-minute sleep hygiene education session and 5 weekly 20-minute check-in calls. Study assessments were conducted at baseline, following treatment (week 7), and at 6-month follow-up (as of May 2023). The primary study outcome was ISI scores; secondary outcomes included sleep diary-based sleep efficiency, 7-night actigraphy (Actiwatch-2), PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) scores, and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores. Outcome assessors were masked to condition. The study was powered at 0.90 to detect a 4-point group difference on the ISI (SD = 6.5) with a sample size of 120 per group (allowance for 15% attrition, alpha = .05, two-tailed). Intention-to-treat linear mixed effects models with random participant and site intercepts and adjustment for baseline ISI and PTSD status were the primary method of analysis. The study was approved by VA Central Institutional Review Board (IRB #2020-0847) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04739228). All participants provided written informed consent before randomization.

Methods
Between March 2021 and November 2022, 240 veterans (M age = 47.3, SD = 12.1; 68% men) were enrolled from outpatient clinics at VA Puget Sound Health Care System (Seattle, WA) and the VA Boston Healthcare System (Boston, MA). Participants met criteria for a DSM-5 diagnosis of chronic insomnia disorder, Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) ≥15, and no current suicidal ideation or psychosis. Veterans with comorbid PTSD (n = 142, 59%) were included to match the intended target population. Of 412 referrals, 240 were assigned to treatment conditions in a 1:1 ratio via computer-generated permuted block randomization (4 per block, stratified by site and PTSD) to cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I; n = 120) or active control group (sleep hygiene education and attention-matched contact; n = 120).
CBT-I consisted of six weekly 50-min individual sessions administered by 14 doctoral-level psychologists (trained to achieve a ≥90% fidelity score on standardized checklist) and comprised sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, and relapse prevention. Sleep hygiene was presented during a single 30-min session, followed by five weekly 20-min follow-up calls for the control group. Participants were evaluated at baseline, post-treatment (7 weeks), and 6-month follow-up (to May 2023). The primary outcome was ISI; secondary outcomes included sleep efficiency from sleep diary, sleep parameters from 7 consecutive nights of actigraphy (Actiwatch-2), PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5), and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Outcome assessors were blinded to group assignment. Sample size (n = 120/arm) was calculated (α = .05, two-tailed, 15% attrition, and 0.90 power) to detect 4-point difference (SD = 6.5) on ISI. Intention-to-treat analyses were performed using linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants and sites and adjustment for baseline ISI and PTSD. Study was approved by the VA Central Institutional Review Board (IRB #2020-0847) and registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04739228). All participants provided written informed consent before randomization.

paper_section_04_luna.text:
A study by the Open Science Collaboration in 2015 showed that published effects in psychology were often less robust than was indicated by the literature, but the findings should not be taken to mean that most initial studies were wrong. In an attempt to replicate 100 papers published in 2008 in *Psychological Science*, the *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, and the *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*, the Open Science Collaboration found that while 97% of the initial studies were statistically significant, only 36% of the replication attempts were. What's more, the average replication effect was about half as big as the original effect size (r = .197 vs. r = .403), which suggests that not finding an effect is sometimes not so much nothing, but a very over-inflated version of it. [Open Science Collaboration, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716)

That's likely a result of selective publication bias (favoring surprise statistically significant results), loose analyses (making unstable, repeatable estimates), and low sample sizes (making estimates even less repeatable). Or maybe the initial studies relied on specific cultural factors, participant types, experimenter expectations, or specifics of procedures, which can be hard to replicate well. That can make a failed direct replication not so much an example of intentional misbehavior or completely misguided theory, but instead of methodological/boundary issues. In fact, 47% of original effect sizes were in the 95% confidence interval of the replication study, and 39% of the results were deemed replicated by replication teams.

But the disparity between initial and replication findings does underscore that statistical significance is not enough for scientific reliability. The big (preregistered!) collaborative effort redirected focus towards issues of power, effect size estimation, transparency, and accumulation of evidence. Perhaps the biggest takeaway is not so much that this study gives one estimate of psychology's "real" replication rate, but an empirical demonstration of ways to inflate unwarranted confidence in published research. To address reproducibility issues, we need to be pre-registering, using bigger samples, making data and materials available, publishing registered reports, and being okay with more null results.

In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration showed that published psychology was not as reliable as the literature implied. This does not mean that most original studies were bogus, but their study does suggest that they were not as reliable as reported. The Open Science Collaboration tried to replicate 100 studies from 2008 in *Psychological Science*, *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* and *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*. Although 97% of original studies found statistically significant results, only 36% of the replication were statistically significant. Further, the average effect size of replications was about half the size of the original effect size (r = .197, vs. r = .403), suggesting that it wasn't always that the true effect was zero, but rather that there was a large overestimate in replication failures. [Open Science Collaboration, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716)

There are several reasons that a direct replication might fail. Because publication bias strongly selects for novel, statistically significant results, and because analyses can easily be adjusted and studies can easily be underpowered, statistically unstable effects can be estimated that would be highly unlikely to repeat. Also, original studies might rely on some combination of cultural, population, experimenter expectation, or protocol idiosyncrasies that cannot readily be replicated. So a direct replication might fail because of boundary conditions or methodological issues, rather than nefarious reasons or a completely wrong theory. Indeed, 47% of original effect sizes are contained within the 95% confidence interval of the replication study, and 39% were considered to have replicated by the teams doing the replication.

Still, the contrast between the original and replication studies makes clear that statistical significance can be a poor indicator of scientific reliability. This study, with its large collaborative, preregistered setup, brought into focus issues of power, effect size estimation, transparency, and cumulative evidence. The real value of the study, then, is not in giving us a single point estimate of what the "true" replication rate for psychology was, but in providing an empirical illustration of how research practices can systematically bias our confidence in published results. Steps to improve the reproducibility of science include preregistration, more power, open data and materials, registered reports, and a higher willingness to share null results.

paper_section_06_glm.text:
Introduction Starting in September 2021, the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) embarked on an unorthodox sequence of interest rate reductions that would shape the most important monetary policy experiment of the contemporary period. In four months, the policy rate was trimmed from 19% to 14%, while consumer price inflation in the year to that month had already reached near 20%. The process continued through 2022 and 2023, culminating in a February 2023 policy rate at 8.5%, even though by October 2022 headline inflation had surged over 80%, the highest ever in Türkiye's republican era. This unconventional sequence was framed in ideological terms, often repeated by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and coded into the government's December 2021 economic plan, as believing that high interest rates cause inflation. This upended traditional monetary theory and colloquially became referred to in Turkish society as " faiz sebep, enflasyon sonuç " (interest is the cause, inflation is the result).

The Turkish experience represents a unique natural experiment, where a large, open economy has voluntarily engaged in a policy experiment the polar opposite of the inflationtargeting mainstream, at a time when international factors, including a post-pandemic pick-up in demand and a commodity price shock from the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, were fueling global inflation pressures. How much of these effects can be attributed to policy is the central empirical question we seek to address.

We make three contributions to the literature: (i) we compile a new monthly data series from January 2010 to December 2023 of CBRT policy actions, Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) price indexes, credit default swaps of sovereigns and USD/TRY exchange rate changes, to depict the timing and transmission of the unorthodox easing cycle; (ii) we use a structural vector autoregression (VAR) model (and also a synthetic control using a weighted sample of emerging markets (e.g., Brazil, South Africa, Poland) to estimate the counterfactual inflation trajectory in the absence of rate cuts; and (iii) we look at the behavioral side, where survey data from both TÜİK consumer expectation surveys and CBRT market expectations polls show how inflation expectations became increasingly unmoored from reality (12-month ahead expectations were more than 60% by mid-2022).

The conclusions shed light on issues like the costs of doing away with institutional monetary arrangements, the exchange rate transmission mechanism in highly dollarized countries, and the political economy of central bank independence. In particular, the Turkish experience-with orthodox policy fully restored under Governor Hafize Gaye Erkan in June 2023, taking the rate from 8.5% to 40% in six months-represents an important natural experiment with lessons well beyond the Turkish case.

Introduction In September 2021, the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) embarked on an unorthodox series of monetary policy rate cuts that would shape one of the most important modern monetary policy experiments. Specifically, the policy rate was cut from 19% to 14% in the span of about four months even though annual CPI inflation was already around 20%. This period (September 2021) was followed by cuts all the way into 2022 and 2023 with the policy rate being as low as 8.5% in February 2023. This was despite the fact that, in October 2022, annual headline inflation surged above 80%, the highest ever in Türkiye's republican history. The intellectual underpinning for these moves, repeatedly emphasized by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and summarized in the December 2021 government's economic program, was a belief that high rates are a source of inflation, reversing standard monetary theory and famously labelled in Turkish as "faiz sebep, enflasyon sonuç" (interest is the cause, inflation is the result). This constitutes an exceptional natural experiment for a large and globally integrated economy to embark on an entirely opposite policy path to the prevailing inflation targeting orthodoxy. This was all the more so at a time of global forces (recovery from post-pandemic demand, commodity price shock caused by the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022) that would raise inflation globally. It is this latter empirical question of separating out domestic policy forces from these global effects that is at the core of this paper. First, to document timing and effects of the unorthodox easing period, we build a monthly database between January 2010 and December 2023 including CBRT policy announcements, Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) price indices, credit default swap rates on sovereign and USD/TRY exchange rate changes. Second, we use a structural vector autoregression model with the support of a synthetic control based on a basket of emerging market economies, including Brazil, South Africa, and Poland, as a comparator to estimate what inflation would have been without rate cuts. Third, we investigate behavioral response: using surveys in TÜİK's consumer expectations as well as CBRT market participants, we find how inflation expectations became increasingly unanchored during this period, rising to above 60% for 12-months ahead by mid-2022. This provides lessons for the current debates on the costs of not having institutional monetary arrangements in place, the pass-through of exchange rates in highly dollarized economies, and the political economy of central bank independence. The Turkish episode which ended with the restoration of orthodox policies under the new Governor Hafize Gaye Erkan as of June 2023 (where rates went from 8.5% to 40% in six months) is therefore a striking natural experiment of lessons beyond the Turkish experience.

paper_section_08_sonnet.text:
Results

The tensile properties were characterized for Ti-6Al-4V specimens produced by LPBF (laser power levels of 150 W, 175 W, 200 W, 225 W and 250 W) on an EOS M290 (fixed process parameters: scan speed, 1200 mm/s; hatch spacing, 0.10 mm; layer thickness, 30 µm). A total of 10 dog bone specimens were produced (ASTM E8 subsize geometry) at each laser power, stress relieved at 650 • C for 3 h in argon, and subsequently loaded to failure on an Instron 5985 at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min. The UTS increased from 1021 ± 18 MPa at 150 W to a maximum of 1147 ± 12 MPa at 200 W and then decreased to 1089 ± 24 MPa at 225 W and 1043 ± 31 MPa at 250 W (mean ± SD, n = 10). The one-way ANOVA analysis indicated that laser power had a significant influence on the UTS (F 4,45 = 26.7, p < 0.001). A post hoc Tukey HSD test further revealed that the 200 W group was significantly different from the rest of the groups (p < 0.01) except for 225 W (p = 0.08). The yield strength also showed a similar trend, with a maximum of 1068 ± 15 MPa at 200 W compared to 948 ± 21 MPa at 150 W. The maximum elongation at break was obtained at 200 W (11.4 ± 0.9%) and exhibited a marked decrease at 250 W (6.2 ± 1.3%) which also corresponded to an increase in the porosity (0.8% vs. 2.9%, micro-CT, respectively) due to the keyhole mode instability at higher energy densities.

The fractographic observations (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) for the 250 W specimens showed the presence of spherical keyhole pores (30-80 µm diameter) mainly located around the crack initiation point, consistent with the decrease in ductility. Conversely, the 150 W specimens showed the presence of lack of fusion defects with irregular morphology, correlated with the decrease in UTS despite a similar overall porosity level (1.1%). Thus, the results demonstrate that the 200 W laser power, within the range investigated, is the most suitable for optimizing the strength-ductility balance in the context of the specific scan parameters adopted in this study.

Results

Tensile behavior of laser powder bed fused (LPBF) Ti-6Al-4V samples was investigated for laser power parameters (150, 175, 200, 225, 250 W) on EOS M290 with scan speed (1200 mm/s), hatch (0.10 mm), and layer height (30 μm) fixed. 10 (ASTM E8 subsize) dog bone samples were 3D printed for each parameter, stress relieved for 3 h at 650 • C under Ar atmosphere, and loaded to failure on Instron 5985 (crosshead speed 1 mm/min).

The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) varied from 1021 ± 18 (150 W) to 1147 ± 12 MPa (200 W), decreasing to 1089 ± 24 MPa (225 W) and 1043 ± 31 MPa (250 W) (mean ± SD, n = 10). A one-way ANOVA found that laser power significantly affected UTS (F(4,45) = 26.7, p < 0.001). Tukey HSD post hoc tests identified the 200 W group was significantly different from the others (p < 0.01), except for 225 W (p = 0.08). Similar to UTS, yield strength peaked at 200 W (1068 ± 15 MPa) compared to 948 ± 21 MPa for 150 W. The elongation at break was highest at 200 W (11.4 ± 0.9%), while 250 W exhibited a severe drop (6.2 ± 1.3%), which was linked to higher porosity (0.8 and 2.9%, micro-CT at 200 and 250 W, respectively) due to keyhole instability caused by higher energy density.

SEM analysis (Zeiss Sigma 300) on fractured surfaces of 250 W samples shows spherical keyhole pores (30-80 µm in diameter) distributed around the area of crack initiation, matching the low ductility. 150 W samples presented lack of fusion defect with irregular shapes, corresponding to lower UTS values despite similar porosity (1.1%). This suggests that 200 W was the best out of the investigated parameters for obtaining optimized strength and ductility with the given scan parameters in the present study.

paper_section_10_luna.text:
Impacts of the British Columbia carbon tax on greenhouse gas emissions in manufacturing plants: The 2019 policy

While British Columbia implemented a revenue-neutral carbon tax in 2008, the provincial carbon tax rate rose to C$40 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in April 2019, resulting in a large price signal for the use of fossil fuels. This paper investigates the impacts of the carbon tax on greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing plants under the 2019 policy. Exploiting confidential plant-level fuel spending, emissions, output, and employment data, we create a panel of greenhouse gas emissions for the manufacturing sector and estimate an augmented difference-in-differences model using plant heterogeneity in tax exposure. We compare more carbon-intensive plants to less exposed plants, controlling for plant and year fixed effects, sector effects and macroeconomic factors.

We find that manufacturing plants' greenhouse gas emissions were lowered by about 4% compared to the counterfactual. This is mainly due to emissions intensity being lowered by about 6% while plant output grew by about 1.8%. These results imply that the emissions fall is not caused by a contraction of the manufacturing sector or plant closures, but rather more output is produced using less fossil fuel energy. This could be linked to investment in energy efficiency and productivity improvements. Moreover, the revenue-neutral nature of the carbon tax (tax revenues were returned to firms via corporate income tax cuts, etc.) may have helped facilitate the shift, as it lowered the cost of emissions abatement investments.

Overall, we find that the BC carbon pricing has caused a detectable reduction in emissions in manufacturing without causing contraction of plant output in aggregate. Our estimates are not necessarily attributable to an independent effect of a new 2019 tax because the carbon tax started in 2008, and the tax rate in 2019 escalated the policy.

Greenhouse-gas emissions from manufacturing plants and British Columbia's carbon tax: evidence from 2019 policy regime

In this study we analyze the impact of British Columbia's carbon tax on greenhouse-gas emissions from manufacturing plants, with a particular focus on 2019 policy regime. While British Columbia has a revenue-neutral carbon tax, which began in 2008, its provincial carbon-tax rate rose to C$40 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in April 2019, sending a large price signal for fossil-fuel consumption. We use confidential plant-level information on fuel spending, emissions, output, and employment to construct a panel of manufacturing emissions. We estimate an augmented difference-in-differences model that leverages variation in plant exposure to carbon tax. The model compares greenhouse-gas emissions from plants more exposed to carbon with those from less exposed, plants while controlling for plants' and years' fixed effects, sectoral trends, and economic conditions. We find that the carbon tax has lowered greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing plants by about 4% compared to the counterfactual. This was primarily due to a decrease in the emissions intensity of about 6% while the plant output rose by about 1.8%. This suggests that the policy has not brought down emissions by contracting manufacturing or through the closure of plants. Rather, firms appear to have responded by generating more output using less energy in fossil fuels, likely through adoption of energy-efficient and productivity-enhancing technologies. The revenue-neutral design of the carbon tax, which reinvested the carbon tax revenues back through, e.g., corporate income tax cuts and other policies, may have helped this by reducing the cost of abatement investments.

Our findings are consistent with the view that British Columbia's carbon-pricing policy led to measurable greenhouse gas emissions reductions from manufacturing without depressing aggregate plant output. However, it is important to note that our estimates do not identify the independent effect of a new carbon tax in 2019, as carbon tax started already in 2008 and the 2019 carbon tax rate was an escalation of an existing program.

Methods In Situ TEM Cell Fabrication Open-cell in situ TEM measurements were carried out in a FEI Titan 80-300 environmental TEM at 300 kV with Gatan OneView camera for continuous imaging at 25 fps. Lithium dendrite deposition was monitored in a nanoscale electrochemical cell assembled in situ in a Hummingbird Scientific electrical biasing TEM holder. We used half-cell configuration with a Li2O-coated lithium metal electrode (∼100 nm thick) obtained by scratching metallic lithium foil (99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) with a tungsten wire for a native Li2O as a solid electrolyte layer. Counter-electrode was a sharp (electrochemically polished) copper wire (99.99%, Alfa Aesar, 250 μm diameter) and brought in contact with the Li2O surface by piezoerically controlled manipulation, with sub-10 nm resolution.

Electrochemical Protocol We employed a Keithley 2400 SourceMeter and an interface to the holder for galvanostatic charging. We calibrated charging currents to effectively correspond to 1 C at nanoscale contact area, which translates to 10-50 A/cm 2 current densities at the electrode-electrolyte interface (the current density was estimated from the measured contact area, 0.01-0.05 μm 2 , as seen in TEM images). In parallel, we supplied a constant −2 V bias to aid nucleation, as in previous open-cell systems.

Imaging Conditions We recorded the evolution of dendrite growth under bright field conditions at 28,000-115,000× magnifications, and kept the total dose below 50 e − /Å 2 /s to avoid artifacts due to electron beam. Control measurements with beam-off confirmed that electron irradiation did not influence the dendrite morphology. The deposition cycles lasted 60-180 s, and we imaged at least twelve independent cells in three experimental runs (March-May 2024) to establish reproducibility.

Data Analysis The velocity of dendrite propagation was determined by frame-by-frame analysis of the growing front with ImageJ (v1.54k). Kymograph analysis provided 5-40 nm/s velocities. Structural properties of dendrite tips were probed with selected area electron diffraction to identify single crystalline Li with body-centered cubic structure along ⟨111⟩ growth direction. All quantitative data are given as mean±standard deviation across the cells.

Methods

In situ TEM cell assembly
In situ TEM of open cell was performed with a FEI Titan 80-300 environmental TEM running at 300 kV with Gatan OneView camera for continuous imaging (frame rate 25 fps). To study lithium dendrite formation, we use a nanoscale electrochemical cell assembled in situ in the electrical biasing TEM holder from Hummingbird Scientific. The electrochemical cell had a half-cell geometry. The Li 2 O-coated lithium metal anode (thickness ∼100 nm) was made by scratching the metallic lithium foil (99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) with a tungsten wire to use natural Li 2 O as the solid electrolyte. The counter electrode was an electrochemically polished sharp copper wire (99.99%, Alfa Aesar, 250 µm in diameter) placed in contact with the Li 2 O surface using piezoerically controlled manipulations with sub-10 nm spatial resolution.

Electrochemical cell operation
A Keithley 2400 SourceMeter was used to provide a galvanostatic charge (the source was connected to the holder). The charging current was adjusted to provide effective 1 C rate at the nanoscale contact point, which results in 10-50 A/cm 2 current density at the electrode-electrolyte interface (the current density was estimated from the contact area 0.01-0.05 µm 2 determined from TEM images). Additionally, a −2 V constant bias was simultaneously applied to facilitate nucleation as in previous open cell cells.

Imaging setup
The lithium dendrite growth was imaged in bright field at magnifications of 28,000-115,000×. The total electron dose was kept lower than 50 e À / Å 2 /s to avoid artefacts induced by electron irradiation. Blanking the electron beam showed that the morphology of lithium dendrites was not affected by electron irradiation. The lithium dendrite deposition period was 60-180 s. At least twelve independent cells from different experimental sessions (March-May 2024) were imaged to check the reproducibility.

Data analysis
Propagation velocity of lithium dendrites was calculated by the frame-by-frame detection of the growth front using ImageJ (v.1.54k) software. The velocities obtained from kymographs are in the range 5-40 nm/s. To characterise the tip structure of lithium dendrites, selected area electron diffraction was used to show single crystalline Li with body-centered cubic structure grows along the ⟨111⟩ direction. The mean ± std is calculated over different cells for the quantitative results.

paper_section_14_sonnet.text:
Limitations

We discuss some key limitations of our federated learning approach in the 12-hospital study: (1) despite applying FedProx (μ=0.01) instead of plain vanilla FedAvg, we still struggled with non-IID data splits among sites. For example, pathology prevalence and class imbalance differed significantly at various sites (e.g., <40 positive cases for pneumothorax at Site 7 (pediatric center in Lyon) versus >2100 cases at Site 3 (level 1 trauma center in Houston in a 14-month data collection period)), potentially explaining the 6.8-point AUC difference (0.91 to 0.843) between top-vs-bottom site performance on held-out local test sets. (2) While we applied some data harmonization preprocessing, we did not fully mitigate scanner/acquisition differences (e.g., 5 out of 12 sites use GE Revolution CT scanners vs. others mix Siemens SOMATOM and Canon Aquilion) and there may still be residual domain shift on reconstruction kernel and slice thickness that our histogram-matching cannot fully eliminate. (3) Our communication setting assumed all 12 sites had stable connections with synchronous rounds (every 48 hours) in a 9-month training period (January to September 2025). In reality, we saw 3 sites drop out at least once during a round, and had to resort to stale client averaging, potentially further disadvantaging sites with unstable connectivity. (4) Although we didn't exchange raw imaging data, we did exchange gradients without formally enforcing differential privacy, and there could be risk of membership inference/gradient inversion attacks, noted by 2 of our IRBs (Houston and Lyon), but not fully addressed within the scope of this work. (5) Our testing is based on held-out site-specific test sets instead of fully external cohorts, so we haven't fully validated generalization to hospitals beyond this 12-site consortium. We should look to add personalization (e.g., per-cluster/site adapter) federated learning and formal privacy analyses before considering for clinical deployment.

Limitations

We discuss some limitations of our federated learning approach for the 12 participating hospitals. First, despite our use of FedProx (μ=0.01) instead of vanilla FedAvg, data distribution among hospitals was still non-IID. For example, the prevalence of the pathologies was highly imbalanced between hospitals. Site 7 (pediatric hospital, Lyon) only had less than 40 positives for pneumothorax in the 14 months of data collection, while Site 3 (level 1 trauma, Houston) had more than 2,100 positives, which may have caused the 6.8-point AUC difference between our best and worst hospital results (0.91 vs. 0.843) on the held-out local test sets. Second, despite our preprocessing harmonization, differences in scanners and acquisitions are still present. 5 of the 12 hospitals use GE Revolution CT, whereas the others employ various Siemens SOMATOM or Canon Aquilion scanners. There may still be reconstruction kernel and slice thickness-related residual domain shift we were not able to fully overcome using our histogram matching approach. Third, our communication setting assumes stable and synchronous communication every 48 hours for all 12 hospitals for the 9-month training period (January-September 2025). In reality, at least 3 hospitals dropped out at some communication rounds, forcing us to resort to stale-client averaging, which might bias against some hospitals with occasionally unstable infrastructures. Fourth, while we did not exchange raw images, we did not formally introduce differential privacy into the gradient sharing and so there is a risk of membership inference attack or gradient inversion attack, which was highlighted by two IRBs we work with (Houston and Lyon), though was beyond the scope of what we were able to address in this study. Finally, instead of a completely external cohort, we tested our approach on held-out test sets by site and thus have not yet demonstrated its generalizability to hospitals not part of this consortium of 12 hospitals. Future work needs to address these with personalized federated learning (e.g. per-cluster/site adapters) and formal privacy quantification before we can consider deployment in clinical settings.

paper_section_16_luna.text:
Introduction The field of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was revolutionized on October 18, 2016, when 10x Genomics introduced the Chromium Single Cell Controller at their headquarters in Pleasanton, California. The Chromium system, which incorporated the use of microfluidic droplets, gel beads with barcodes and unique molecular identifiers, enabled high-throughput profiling of thousands of cells simultaneously, marking a significant leap in throughput compared with the prior low-throughput, plate-based techniques (e.g. Smart-seq2) at lower costs and with less effort. The release of the Chromium system coincided with the launch of the Human Cell Atlas project on October 13–14, 2016, at the Wellcome Trust in London, marking the commencement of a major initiative to catalogue cell types and states in the human body on a large scale. [10x Genomics](https://s28.q4cdn.com/592666581/files/doc_news/2016/10/18/10x-genomics-announces-new-low-cost-single-cell-instrument.pdf), [Human Cell Atlas](https://www.humancellatlas.org/event/human-cell-atlas-launch-meeting/)

In the years following, scRNA-seq has grown not only in scale, but also in its biological scope. Technical advances in droplet protocols, sequencing strategies and bioinformatics tools now enable scRNA-seq experiments to target hundreds of thousands to millions of cells, with single-nucleus RNA-seq further broadening the scope of scRNA-seq to include frozen samples, archives and complex tissues that are difficult to isolate and dissociate. Alongside this, transcriptomes have been profiled alongside other data types, including chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, protein expression levels and immune receptor sequences. These multimodal profiles have uncovered cellular states and developmental lineages, tumour heterogeneity and tissue-specific regulatory networks with a granularity that was previously unattainable using bulk RNA sequencing. [Nature Reviews Genetics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-023-00580-2)

Most recently, spatial transcriptomics has emerged as a new technology to overcome a key limitation of the dissociative scRNA-seq: the loss of spatial information. Spatial profiling preserves the location of gene expression, thus bridging the gap between molecular cell types and spatial tissue architecture, including cell-cell interactions. These advances in high-throughput sequencing, multi-omics and spatial technologies, as well as more advanced statistical and machine learning tools, have propelled scRNA-seq from a sophisticated technique for measurement into a key methodology for generating cellular atlases and for studying disease.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has evolved rapidly since the introduction of the Chromium Single Cell Controller by 10x Genomics in Pleasanton, CA, on October 18, 2016. Chromium introduced a powerful combination of microfluidic droplet technology with barcoded gel beads and unique molecular identifiers that allowed for the high-throughput profiling of thousands of individual cells simultaneously, vastly boosting sample throughput, lowering the cost and effort of transcriptomic profiling compared to previous methods such as plate-based assays (e.g., Smart-seq2). This technological breakthrough paralleled the launch of the Human Cell Atlas initiative at the Wellcome Trust in London (October 13–14, 2016), a grand plan for large-scale characterization of the human cell types and states in a variety of tissues. [10x Genomics](https://s28.q4cdn.com/592666581/files/doc_news/2016/10/18/10x-genomics-announces-new-low-cost-single-cell-instrument.pdf), [Human Cell Atlas](https://www.humancellatlas.org/event/human-cell-atlas-launch-meeting/)

Single-cell RNA sequencing has evolved in both breadth and depth. Refinements in droplet chemistries, sequencing and computational methods have allowed scaling to hundreds of thousands or even millions of cells. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing can profile tissues, even those that are frozen or archived, or complex and hard to isolate intact. Concomitant technical progress has allowed the pairing of transcriptomic data with other types of molecular information, such as chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, protein expression and immune receptor sequences. By providing complementary data in these modalities, scientists can better define cellular states and developmental stages, tumor diversity and specific tissue regulatory elements that cannot be directly measured with bulk RNA sequencing. [Nature Reviews Genetics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-023-00580-2)

Recently, with the advent of spatial transcriptomics, a major drawback of the dissociative scRNA-seq has been overcome by retaining a sense of the physical locations of gene expression events. This combination of spatial and molecular identities has linked molecular data to spatial and cell–cell contexts. The combination of high-throughput sequencing, multi-modal approaches, spatial measurements, coupled with an increasingly wide range of statistical and machine learning approaches has transformed single-cell RNA sequencing from a niche measurement technique to a general measurement platform for cellular atlases and disease.

Results

The 5-ResNet-50 ensemble had a mean accuracy of 91.4% in the ISIC 2020 holdout test set (n = 3,326 dermoscopic images), outperforming all individual models. The most accurate individual model scored 89.1% and the lowest model scored 86.7%, demonstrating that the ensemble boost (2.3% accuracy) over the best single model is from averaging. The ensemble's sensitivity in malignant melanoma detection was 88.9% (95% CI: 86.4-91.1%) and specificity was 92.6% (95% CI: 90.8-94.2%). The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve area under the curve (AUROC) score of the ensemble was 0.941 versus a range of 0.908-0.927 in individual models.

Further analysis of misclassifications found that 61.3% of false negative errors come from dermoscopic images scored as ambiguous or low-contrast by 2 board certified dermatologists (blinded, Cohen's κ = 0.71), especially for acral melanomas and dark nevi with regression patterns. False positive errors are most frequent in seborrheic keratoses with inflammatory halos or recurrent nevi, which are known challenges in dermoscopy.

When analyzing the attention maps (class activation Grad-CAM), we found that the 5-ResNet-50 ensemble focused on pigment network patterns and aberrant streaks in 78.4% of correct malignant cases, while individual models were more likely to focus on noise artifacts like ruler and gel bubbles (12.1% of Grad-CAM heatmaps compared to 4.6% in the ensemble) and thus less focused when averaged together.

Finally, when analyzing accuracy stratified by Fitzpatrick skin type subgroups, we found no statistically significant decrease in accuracy for skin types IV to VI (90.2%, p = 0.18, DeLong test), but the small sample size (n = 281) may limit statistical power. The overall training time for the 5-fold cross validation (on 26,604 image training split) was 14 hours on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU per fold, and overall training + inference time was 96 hours. The ensemble model accuracy (while still close) did not surpass the 92.8% accuracy of the consensus panel of 76 dermatologists on the same test set (n = 3,326, McNemar's test p = 0.06). The results suggest that ResNet-50 ensembles represent a strong and comparable baseline to dermatologists for triage of melanoma, but also point out remaining weaknesses when faced with challenging and ambiguous lesions.

Results
Ensemble averaging of five ResNet-50 networks produced an average test classification accuracy of 91.4% (held-out ISIC 2020 test split, n = 3,326 dermoscopic images) which outperformed all constituent baseline networks. The top-performing network had an accuracy of 89.1%, and the lowest-performing network an accuracy of 86.7%. The ensemble, therefore, performed 2.3 percentage points better than the top network alone. Sensitivity for detection of malignant melanoma was 88.9% (95% CI 86.4-91.1%), with specificity at 92.6% (95% CI 90.8-94.2%). The AUC (area under receiver operating characteristic curve) of the ensemble was 0.941, compared to individual networks of 0.908-0.927. Analysis of misclassifications found that 61.3% of false negatives were on images that had been called equivocal or low contrast lesions by two blinded board-certified dermatologists (Cohen's κ = 0.71), especially acral melanomas and highly pigmented nevi with regression structures. False positives were often found on images of seborrheic keratoses with inflammatory halos and recurrent nevi, reflecting common pitfalls in dermoscopy. Activation of attention with Grad-CAM (class activation mapping) found that the ensemble focused on pigment network and abnormal streaking patterns for 78.4% of correct classifications of malignant lesions. Individual networks were more likely to focus on image artifacts such as rulers and gel bubbles (12.1% of Grad-CAM heatmaps compared to 4.6% for the ensemble), perhaps reducing attention to spurious features through averaging. Analysis by Fitzpatrick skin type found no statistically significant loss of accuracy in skin types IV-VI (accuracy 90.2%, p = 0.18 by DeLong test), although numbers are small (n = 281). Training time for 5-fold cross-validation of 26,604 image training set was about 14 hours per fold using a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Total training and inference time was 96 hours. Performance of the ensemble was close but not better than the 76-dermatologist consensus panel accuracy of 92.8% when tested on the same test set (n = 3,326, McNemar's test p = 0.06). These findings show that ensembling ResNet-50 networks is a stable, dermatologist-level starting point for melanoma triage, but suggests remaining challenges with ambiguous lesion morphologic types.
